ANSWER Q3: The conclusion that Tier-3 failures are generally subthreshold activation failures rather than failures to represent harmfulness would lose support. Near-chance AUC would instead suggest that harmful and harmless instructions are not reliably distinguished internally.

ANSWER Q4: No. Aya’s Tier-4 ASR is worse under code-switching than under standard translation, so testing only standard translation would miss its worst-case vulnerability.

ANSWER Q5: No. Scottish Gaelic uses the Latin script, so transliteration provides little or no additional perturbation, and Qwen’s reported transliteration ASR is not higher than its standard-translation ASR.

ANSWER Q6: Not by itself. If prompt length systematically separated the two classes, a probe could obtain high AUC from length-related activation features rather than an internal representation of harmfulness.

ANSWER Q7: Contradicted. The reported cross-language relationships are not uniformly negative across all three models; stronger instruction-level harm signals generally accompany, rather than universally oppose, stronger downstream refusal signals.

ANSWER Q8: No. High probe AUC only shows that harmfulness is decodable; Tier-1 standard translations generally also trigger refusal, so there is no behavioral evidence that the signal remains below the activation threshold.

ANSWER Q9: Qwen would be the safest choice on the reported standard-translation and code-switching results. It has the lowest overall Tier-4 attack success among the three models under those attacks, although it is not invulnerable.

ANSWER Q10: It would conflict with Llama’s comparatively weak multilingual safety behavior—especially its relatively high attack success as language resources decline. A largest cross-lingual margin would predict stronger transfer of the English safety signal, not that vulnerability.

ANSWER Q11: No substantive change would be expected. When the target language is English, replacing selected English spans with their English translations leaves the prompt effectively identical to the English baseline.

ANSWER Q12: It would cease to differ if the translation process produced the same idiomatic wording as standard translation rather than literal, source-syntax-preserving “translationese.” The two attacks would then present essentially the same prompt distribution.

ANSWER Q13: It would undermine the claim that non-English harm representations remain geometrically separated from the English safety subspace through late layers. Sharply shrinking angles would instead indicate late-layer convergence onto a shared representation.

ANSWER Q14: ASR can treat the absence of a recognizable refusal as success even when the output is irrelevant, incoherent, merely translational, or otherwise not genuinely harmful. Automated judging and back-translation can therefore count false-positive “compliance.”

ANSWER Q15: Contradicted. Transliteration raises ASR for many script-changing conditions, but not for every language-model pair, particularly where the language already uses Latin script or transliteration does not meaningfully alter the prompt.

ANSWER Q16: The conclusion that transliteration’s bimodality is a general, model-independent script effect would be weakened. An effect confined to one model could instead reflect that model’s tokenizer, training distribution, or alignment procedure.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The paper shows that code-switching changes behavior and internal harm/refusal signals, but it does not directly identify or causally manipulate a language-identification routing mechanism.

ANSWER Q18: It would likely bias Tier-4 ASR upward. Garbling can erase recognizable refusal language, causing safe or malformed responses to be classified as non-refusals and hence as successful attacks.

ANSWER Q19: No. Swahili is an outlier rather than a clean example of the typical Tier-3 subthreshold pattern, so its probe and projection behavior should be checked before applying a \(b_0\)-boosting remedy; weak harm representation would require a different fix.

ANSWER Q20: Transliteration. For sufficiently resourced non-Latin-script languages such as Korean or Arabic, rendering the prompt in another script most directly exploits the reported script-conditioned safety gap and often produces the largest ASR increase.

# Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety

Chigozirim Ifebi

Affiliation: California Institute of Technology

Correspondence to: cifebi@caltech.edu

  
Brent Kong

Affiliation: California Institute of Technology

Correspondence to: bkong@caltech.edu

  
Ayushi Mehrotra

Affiliation: California Institute of Technology

###### Abstract

Safety alignment in large language models remains brittle across languages: prompts reliably refused in English can elicit harmful compliance in non-English and low-resource settings. We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 perturbation types (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese), together with a geometric analysis of refusal failure across language tiers in the residual stream. Each attack type yields a distinct vulnerability profile: transliteration vulnerability tracks script identity, code-switching retains effectiveness through the lowest-resource tier, and all models show the same abrupt change in safety regime between Tiers 2 and 3. Mechanistically, low-resource failures coincide with harmfulness subspaces that are misaligned with their English counterparts and with projections onto the refusal directions that fall below threshold, while the refusal directions themselves continue to transfer. Valid safety evaluation therefore has to condition on script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage rather than on English-only testing. The benchmark and analysis code is at https://github.com/Brentkong/Minionese-Comprehensive-Benchmark-and-Mechanistic-Study-of-Multilingual-LLM-Safety.git.

###### Keywords: 

jailbreaking, multilingual jailbreaking, mechanistic interpretability

This paper contains harmful data and model-generated content
that can be offensive in nature.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are deployed across languages, scripts, and user populations, yet their reliability in non-English and low-resource contexts is systematically lower, owing to disparities in training data, evaluation coverage, and representational fidelity (Pava and others, 2025). Users in lower-resource language communities consequently receive weaker safety guarantees than English users, a disparity that current evaluation frameworks rarely surface. Aggregate jailbreak rates do not localize where safety enforcement degrades under multilingual distribution shift; a mechanistic account is needed.

Multilingual prompting amplifies jailbreak success (Deng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), but the corresponding internal failure modes remain poorly characterized. In English-centric settings, refusal is mediated by a low-dimensional direction in activation space: ablating it suppresses refusal on harmful requests and adding it induces refusal on benign ones (Arditi et al., 2024). Safety is thereby a geometric property of internal encodings that can, in principle, be audited and repaired rather than only measured at the output.

Refusal across safety-aligned languages is likewise mediated by a single direction (Wang et al., 2025), and multilingual jailbreaks persist despite this shared mechanism because harmful and harmless prompts are less cleanly separated in non-English representation spaces (Wang et al., 2025).

We do not re-establish the universality of refusal directions. Our question is narrower: under meaning-preserving perturbations of the kind an attacker would employ, where does the refusal trigger fail, and what is the geometry of that failure? We study code-switching, transliteration, and translationese in addition to standard translation, across 18 languages and 4 resource tiers.

Following the instruction-token / post-instruction-token decomposition of Zhao et al. (2025), we measure the residual stream along a harmfulness axis and a refusal axis separately. Principal angles between non-English and English harmfulness subspaces approach orthogonality at Tier 4; at Tier 3, harmfulness remains linearly decodable at the instruction token while the projection onto the refusal direction stays below the decision threshold (subthreshold activation). Transliteration of non-Latin-script languages is associated with semantic recovery failure, and code-switching with disruption of language-identification routing, the latter consistent with its effectiveness across all resource tiers.

Script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage are therefore required variables in safety evaluation and alignment. Our contributions are as follows:

1.

We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark
spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated
perturbation types, with harmful-harmless prompt pairs enabling per-attack-type
mechanistic analysis that prior translation-only benchmarks do not support.

2.

We present an empirical evaluation across three instruction-tuned models
showing that each attack type produces a distinct, replicable vulnerability
profile: transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned, code-switching
maintains effectiveness through Tier 4, and a sharp safety regime transition
between Tiers 2 and 3 is consistent across all models.

3.

We analyze harmfulness and refusal components of the residual stream via linear probes, silhouette separation, principal angles, harm–refusal decomposition, and an activation-domain refusal cone, giving mechanistic evidence for two failure modes, subthreshold activation and semantic recovery failure.

## 2 Related Work

##### Multilingual jailbreak benchmarks.

Deng et al. (2024) showed that low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages. Later benchmarks tightened evaluation standards (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024) but remain English-only. Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) jailbreak models by fine-tuning on harmless low-resource data; Poppi et al. (2025) find that safety degradation transfers cross-lingually through roughly 20% of model parameters. Closest to ours, Wang et al. (2025) build a 14-language translated-prompt dataset, show that refusal directions transfer across languages, and attribute persistent jailbreaks to insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English spaces. Minionese treats manipulation type (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) as an independent variable, which existing benchmarks do not.

##### The refusal mechanism.

Arditi et al. (2024) identify a single low-dimensional refusal direction. Wollschläger et al. (2025) replace it with multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones. Zhao et al. (2025) separate a harmfulness direction at the instruction token from a refusal direction at the post-instruction token and show causally that the two dissociate under jailbreaks. We carry this decomposition into the multilingual setting. See Appendix A for an extended
discussion of each thread.

## 3 Minionese: A Granular Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmark

Prior multilingual benchmarks take language identity as the primary variable and restrict perturbations to standard translation. Minionese fixes semantic content and varies the type of linguistic manipulation.

##### Base corpus.

Minionese is built on the 385 harmful prompts from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023). Each harmful prompt is paired with a harmless counterpart obtained by substituting harmful phrases with semantically parallel benign ones using ChatGPT’s GPT-5.4, giving 385 harmful-harmless pairs. Human reviewers verified for every harmless prompt that sentence structure and length were preserved, so that the members of a pair are not distinguishable by token-level surface features.

##### Languages and resource tiers.

The 18 languages are grouped into four tiers by training-data availability in contemporary LLMs:

•

Tier 1 (high-resource): English, Spanish, Chinese, German,
French

•

Tier 2 (mid-high resource): Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese

•

Tier 3 (mid-low resource): Turkish, Indonesian, Hindi, Swahili

•

Tier 4 (low-resource): Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní,
Javanese

Translations use the Google Translate API. Every attack type is applied to every pair in every language, for $385\times 2\times 4\times 18=55,440$
prompts in total. Examples are given in Section E of the appendix.

### 3.1 Attack Types

##### Standard translation.

Both members of the pair are translated in full into the target language; this matches prior multilingual jailbreak studies and serves as the baseline condition.

##### Code-switching.

Each pair is tokenized into words and punctuation; the contiguous span on which harmful and harmless prompts differ is identified, and only the alphabetic tokens within it are translated into the target language. All shared context outside that span remains English.

##### Transliteration.

Prompts are first fully translated and then rendered phonetically in another script, discarding native orthography while preserving pronunciation. Non-Romance languages are romanized into Latin characters; Romance languages are rendered in Latin-Cyrillic. The condition probes refusal behavior keyed to script or token identity rather than to semantic content.

##### Translationese.

The English prompt is translated into the target language, back-translated into English, and translated into the target language again, for three translation steps in total. The final prompt is in the target language and carries the surface statistics of machine-translated text.

## 4 Evaluation

Three models are evaluated on all 18 languages and 4 perturbation types for attack success rate (ASR), response coherence, and safety regime distribution, via response generation, coherence filtering, and back-translated WildGuard scoring.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### 4.1.1 Models and Inference

We evaluate Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Aya-Expanse-8B with greedy decoding (temperature $=0$ ) and a maximum of 512 new tokens.

#### 4.1.2 Coherence Filtering

For each (model, language, perturbation) triple we generate responses to all 385 harmful and 385 harmless prompts. Coherence is assessed via language identification (langdetect) and Unicode validity; a response is incoherent if (i) its detected language is neither the target language nor English; (ii) language identification confidence is below 0.3; (iii) Unicode validity is below 0.8; or (iv) it is shorter than 20 characters. Incoherent responses are excluded from ASR. Coherence rates are at or near 1.0 in every condition (see Section 4.2).

#### 4.1.3 Attack Success Rate Measurement

WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) is the primary safety judge. Non-English responses are back-translated into English before scoring to offset WildGuard’s reduced reliability on non-English text. A response counts as an attack success if WildGuard does not classify it as a refusal, and ASR is computed per (language, perturbation, model) cell:

| | $\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{model}(x)\ \text{is compliant}\right],$
| | (1)

where $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}$ is the set of harmful prompts and
$\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator function. We report ASR per language, per perturbation, and per tier, and
$\Delta$ ASR relative to the English baseline.

### 4.2 Results

Figure 1: ASR by language and perturbation type, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Heatmaps for
Aya and Qwen are in Appendix B.

Figure 1 gives per-language, per-attack-type ASR for Llama; Qwen and Aya are qualitatively similar (Appendix B).

#### 4.2.1 Attack Type and Tier Profiles

##### Standard translation and translationese follow a tier gradient.

For both attack types, ASR rises as resource level falls on all three models. Under standard translation, Llama mean ASR increases from approximately 8% in Tier 1 to over 70% in Tiers 3–4 (Yoruba
100%, Zulu 97%, Scottish Gaelic 98%). Qwen shows the same trend (Swahili
96%, Scottish Gaelic 90%, Yoruba 75%); Aya's gradient is shallower, except for Swahili at 95%. Translationese exceeds standard translation at mid-resource languages, most strongly for Korean (14% vs. 51% on Aya) and Hindi (15% vs. 48% on Llama), consistent with weakened harmfulness detection upstream of refusal under the more naturalistic surface forms produced by round-trip translation.

##### Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned.

For non-Latin-script languages in Tiers 1–2, transliteration yields the highest ASR of any attack: Korean 98% on Aya and 99% on Llama; Chinese
97% on Llama; Arabic 84% on Aya; Hindi 99% on Llama. For Latin-script and very-low-resource Tier-4 languages it falls to near zero (French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on both Aya and
Qwen). On Qwen, $\Delta$ ASR is negative for Yoruba ( $-38\%$ ), Russian ( $-48\%$ ),
and Scottish Gaelic ( $-44\%$ ). The bimodality replicates on all three models and tracks script identity, not resource level.

##### Code-switching produces the most tier-stable attack profile.

Code-switching retains moderate-to-high ASR across all tiers and models. At Tier 4, where other attacks are near zero, it reaches Yoruba (62% on Aya, 82% on Llama), Zulu (62% on Aya, 85% on Llama),
and Guaraní (42% on Aya, 46% on Llama). Its tier gradient is much shallower than that of standard translation, as expected if the operative failure is language-identification routing rather than semantic representation quality.

##### The safety regime transitions sharply between Tiers 2 and 3.

In Tiers 1–2, refusal predominates: Llama 80% refuse in Tier 1 and 75% in Tier 2; Qwen 80% and 88%; Aya 75% in
both. At Tier 3, Llama falls to 31%
refuse, Qwen to 50%, and Aya to 31%, and Aya reaches 95% comply by Tier 4. A mixed regime is almost absent for every model and tier, which favors a threshold in refusal activation over continuous degradation.

#### 4.2.2 Cross-Model Consistency

Qualitative profiles agree across models while absolute magnitudes differ. The rank ordering of attack types by mean ASR is stable: transliteration dominates for Tier-1 and Tier-2 non-Latin-script languages, code-switching dominates at Tier 4, and standard translation and translationese form the most closely matched, generally lowest-ASR pair, pointing to structural properties of transformer safety circuits rather than model-specific training artifacts.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is the most broadly vulnerable model, with Tier-4 standard translation mean ASR approaching 80%, against approximately 55% for Qwen and 35% for Aya. Transliteration bimodality reproduces on all three architectures (Appendix B) and is attributable to the romanization operation itself.

## 5 Geometric Analysis of Refusal

We operationalize the upstream/downstream distinction through linear probing, subspace construction, and cross-lingual transfer analysis. Unless stated otherwise, all analyses in this section use the standard_translation attack type.

### 5.1 Preliminaries

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with $L$ layers and hidden dimension $d$ . We
extract residual stream activations $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at the last post-instruction token position $t^{*}$ for each input
$\mathbf{x}$ . For language $\lambda$ and layer $\ell$ , we define harmful and
harmless activation sets $\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ and
$\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ from our paired benchmark.

##### Harmfulness subspace.

For each $(\lambda,\ell)$ , we train a logistic regression probe and stack weights
across harm categories into $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{C}|}$ , where $\mathcal{C}$ is comprised of “all “ and “unknown” categories derived from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ is the
column space of the top- $k$ right singular vectors of
$\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , with $k$ chosen to retain $\geq 95\%$ of
spectral mass.

##### Refusal direction.

$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is computed from English activations by contrasting refused ( $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}$ ) and complied
( $\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}$ ) sets:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}\|_{2}}$
| | (2)

##### Failure classification.

Following Zhao et al. (2025), harm and refusal components are separated and each $(\lambda,\ell)$ pair is labelled upstream, downstream, or mixed. Refusal is modelled as
$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)\top}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})>\tau^{(\ell)}$ with $\tau^{(\ell)}=0.95$; a language exhibits subthreshold activation when harmful activations remain below $\tau^{(\ell)}$ in the presence of nontrivial harm signal.

### 5.2 Results

Figure 2: Harmful-harmless separation in activation space (silhouette score)
across languages and layers, all three models using standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmful-harmless separation degrades with resource tier.

Figure 2 gives silhouette scores (Rousseeuw, 1987)
in the harmfulness-subspace projection. Tier-1 and Tier-2 languages keep high, stable separation at all layers on all three models. Separation declines from Tier 3 onward, identically across architectures. Guaraní (gn) reaches near-zero and negative scores at all layers on every model, the sharpest degeneration in the benchmark. Swahili (sw) scores well below the other Tier-3 languages on all three models, matching its anomalously high ASR (Section 4.2).

The tier ordering is fixed by mid-network depth and does not change thereafter; separation is not recovered in later layers for lower-resource languages. The Tier-1-to-Tier-4 gap is consistent across architectures and largest for Aya.

Figure 3: Linear probe AUC for harmfulness detection across all layers using standard_translation attack type
(category all; chance $=0.5$ ).

##### Probe AUC confirms subthreshold activation as the dominant failure mode.

Figure 3 reports 5-fold cross-validated probe AUC at every layer. For Tiers 1–3, all three models reach AUC ${\geq}0.85$ from early layers onward; degradation is confined to Tier 4, with Yoruba and Zulu approaching chance in late layers on all models.

For Tier-3 languages, AUC stays high in exactly the conditions where ASR is elevated (subthreshold activation). The Tier-4 decline toward chance corresponds instead to semantic recovery failure.

Figure 4: Principal angle between non-English and English safety subspaces as a
function of normalized layer depth, per tier and model for standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmfulness subspaces are not cross-lingually universal.

Figure 4 plots the first principal angle
$\theta^{(\ell)}_{\lambda,1}$ between non-English and English harmfulness
subspaces against normalized layer depth. No tier approaches
$0^{\circ}$ : Tier-1 languages sit at $40$ – $65^{\circ}$
depending on the model, and Tier-4 languages at near-orthogonality
( ${\sim}85$ – $90^{\circ}$ ) on all three architectures. Angles are roughly constant in depth, with no late-layer cross-lingual realignment. Qwen has the smallest mean angles ( ${\approx}60$ – $65^{\circ}$ ), in line with its higher Tier-4 silhouette scores in Figure 2.

Angles increase monotonically from Tier 1 to Tier 4, paralleling the ASR tier gradient; an English-derived $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ mediates refusal in language $\lambda$ only to the extent that the harm signal in $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ projects onto it.

##### Harm and refusal signals are geometrically decoupled.

Figure 9 (Appendix C) gives four views of the harmfulness-refusal decomposition for all three models. Harm and refusal component norms are weakly correlated and widely scattered on every model. Swahili, Scottish Gaelic, Yoruba, and Zulu each show instances, across the models, of harm norms disproportionately large relative to their refusal components. For Aya and Llama, the per-language contrastive harm signal
$\sigma_{\mathrm{harm}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{inst}}$ correlates strongly and negatively with
the refusal signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{refusal}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{post}}$ ( $r=-0.79$ for Aya, $r=-0.68$ for Llama), whereas Qwen shows a positive correlation, $r=+0.53$ . Whether Tier-4 languages cluster in the low-harm, variable-refusal region across further models remains open.

Layer-wise failure labels are predominantly mixed for all three models. A small number of upstream labels occur, all in Tier-4 languages. No downstream labels occur for any model.

##### Synthesis.

All three models give the same picture. Tier-1 inputs show both clean harmful-harmless separation and adequate projection onto $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$. Tier-3–4 inputs lose one or both. The dominant label is mixed: harmfulness is decodable at the instruction token, but the subspace carrying it is misaligned and low-rank, and its intersection with
$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ is too small to cross $\tau^{(\ell)}$. In the lowest-resource Tier-4 languages, probe AUC additionally falls toward chance. In no condition is $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ itself suppressed.

### 5.3 Refusal Cone Structure and Cross-Lingual Representational Independence

Sections 5.1–5.2 use a single mean-difference direction $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ .
Wollschläger et al. (2025) show for English that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional concept cones. We extend this to the multilingual setting with (i) activation-domain cone optimisation, fitting the basis on cached residual activations instead of gradient-based model interventions, and (ii) Cross-Lingual Representational Independence (CL-RepInd).

##### Cone optimisation.

Let $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ be an orthonormal basis for an
$N$ -dimensional refusal cone, initialised with $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ , and minimise

| | $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})=&-\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})}_{\text{EN margin}}+\lambda_{\rm cone}\underbrace{\vphantom{\frac{1}{N}}\bigl({\rm ReLU}(\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})-\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i-1}))\bigr)}_{\text{cone spread}}\\
&-\lambda_{\rm xl}\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\Delta_{\lambda}(b_{i})}_{\text{CL margin}},\end{split}$
| | (3)

where $\Delta_{\lambda}(b)$ is the harmful–harmless margin along $b$ for language
$\lambda$ and $\Lambda$ is the set of non-English languages. Optimisation is Stiefel-manifold
gradient ascent for 400 steps ( $\eta\!=\!0.05$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{cone}}\!=\!5$ ,
$\lambda_{\mathrm{xl}}\!=\!1$ ), with $N\!\in\!\{1,\ldots,5\}$ and
$N\!=\!5$ canonical. CL-RepInd is the Pearson correlation between the per-language margin vectors of two basis directions.

##### Results (Figures 5–6,
Appendix D).

$b_{0}$ attains English margins of $9.7$ (Qwen), $6.1$ (Aya), and $2.8$ (Llama), and cross-lingual margins of $5.3$ , $3.8$ , and
$0.75$ respectively. Mean margins decay steeply beyond $b_{0}$ ; by dimension three the minimum sampled cone margin is near zero for all models. Cross-lingual margins for $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ are near zero or negative (Aya $b_{1}$ : $-0.4$ ; Qwen $b_{1}$ :
$-0.9$ ). CL-RepInd gives $|r|<0.2$ among $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ , each tied to language clusters: on Aya, $b_{1}$ has negative margins for Japanese and Korean; on Qwen, $b_{2}$ isolates Arabic. Cross-lingually, refusal is effectively one-dimensional.

$b_{0}$ margins are near zero for Tier-4 languages on all three models, placing the Tier-4 failure upstream of the refusal axis, at the harmfulness-detection stage rather than in the refusal subspace.

## 6 Discussion

The failure modes are distinct and depend on manipulation type. Semantic recovery failure predominates in transliteration of non-Latin-script languages and in very-low-resource Tier-4 languages; subthreshold activation predominates in Tier-3 standard translation and translationese; code-switching corresponds to disruption of language-identification routing, independent of representation quality, consistent with its cross-tier robustness. The geometric analyses of Section 5 use standard translation; the attribution for transliteration and code-switching rests on the behavioral profiles of Section 4.2.

##### Refusal geometry is effectively one-dimensional cross-lingually.

Per Section 5.3, the English refusal cone is multi-dimensional, as in
Wollschläger et al. (2025), but only $b_{0}$
transfers cross-lingually; $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ carry near-zero or
negative cross-lingual margins on all three models and encode
script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. Contrastive activation addition and refusal subspace projection should generalise across languages only along $b_{0}$, and interventions along higher cone dimensions may degrade non-English safety. The per-language margin heatmaps mirror the script-conditioned bimodality of Section 4.2, suggesting a common geometric origin.

##### Tier-4 failure is upstream, not directional.

Near-zero $b_{0}$ margins for Tier-4 languages locate the failure in the harm representation, not in the orientation of the refusal axis; remediation for these languages must target harmfulness detection. Swahili is a Tier-3 outlier with consistently near-zero $b_{0}$ margins on all models, indicating that fluency and safety alignment can decouple during training and that resource tier is an imperfect proxy for safety risk.

##### Cross-model consistency.

The tier gradient, script-conditioned bimodality, geometric decoupling of harm and refusal, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal all replicate across Llama, Qwen, and Aya, implicating structural properties of transformer safety alignment under multilingual distribution shift rather than model-specific artifacts. Extended limitations and future work directions
are in Appendix F.

## 7 Conclusion

Minionese spans 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types and was evaluated on three instruction-tuned models. Attack-type profiles are structurally distinct and irreducible to resource level: transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned, code-switching remains effective through Tier 4, and translationese consistently raises standard translation ASR. A sharp safety regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3 replicates on all three models.

The geometric analysis gives a two-stage account consistent across all three architectures. Harmful content in low-resource languages occupies a thinner, less linearly separable subspace whose principal angles with the English harmfulness subspace approach orthogonality at Tier 4. Where a usable harm representation exists, its projection onto the refusal direction frequently stays below the decision threshold (subthreshold activation), so internally harm-encoding inputs still yield compliant responses.

In the refusal cone, the English cone is multi-dimensional but cross-linguistically thin: only $b_{0}$ transfers, while secondary directions carry near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins and appear to encode script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. Only $b_{0}$ -aligned additions are expected to raise refusal cross-lingually; interventions along higher cone dimensions risk degrading non-English safety.

The consistency of these failure modes across Llama, Qwen, and Aya, which differ in multilingual training regime, bears directly on the design of safety audits and governance frameworks for global deployment. English-only safety testing, or testing that ignores perturbation type, script family, and per-language alignment coverage, does not surface the vulnerability profile documented here.

## Impact Statement

This paper aims to improve the safety and equity of multilingual LLM deployment by exposing how models that refuse harmful prompts in English may still comply in lower-resource languages or under perturbations such as transliteration, code-switching, and translationese. By introducing Minionese and analyzing these failures mechanistically, we provide diagnostic tools for multilingual safety evaluation, red-teaming, and future alignment interventions. While this work makes vulnerable language–attack combinations accessible, we mitigate this risk by emphasizing failure mechanisms rather than optimized attack recipes or harmful completions. Overall, we believe that measuring these gaps is necessary for responsible deployment, since English-only safety testing can obscure risks faced by non-English and low-resource language communities.

## Appendix A Extended Related Work

### A.1 Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmarks and the Low-Resource Safety Gap

Deng et al. (2024) first characterized the cross-lingual fragility of safety alignment systematically: low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages in both unintentional and intentional jailbreak scenarios. Their benchmark, MultiJail, is restricted to standard translation. Zou et al. (2023) provide AdvBench, the English harmful-behavior benchmark on which later multilingual studies build; their greedy-gradient suffix attack shows aligned models to be adversarially brittle even in their primary training language. Chao et al. (2024) address reproducibility in jailbreak evaluation with a standardized, open-sourced benchmark and unified threat model, also English-only. None of these specifies the multilingual dimension.

Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) show that fine-tuning on entirely harmless data in a new low-resource language suffices to jailbreak a model, and attribute the effect to late-layer pivots that override safety-critical representations with language-fidelity objectives, an indirect instance of the semantic-recovery failure studied here under transliteration. Poppi et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning attacks generalize cross-lingually: compromising one language degrades safety in others, with only approximately 20% of weight parameters implicated, indicating that safety information is largely language-agnostic at the parameter level.

Wang et al. (2025) construct a 14-language dataset of translated harmful prompts and show that English refusal directions transfer with near-perfect effectiveness, with refusal vectors approximately parallel in activation space; they attribute persistent cross-lingual jailbreaks, despite this universal direction, to insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English languages.

Minionese varies the type of linguistic manipulation (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese) at fixed semantic content instead of treating language identity as the sole independent variable, enabling per-attack-type mechanistic analysis unsupported by MultiJail or PolyRefuse and exposing attack-type-specific representational failure modes.

### A.2 The Refusal Mechanism in Large Language Models

Arditi et al. (2024) showed, in English, that refusal in aligned LLMs is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction: ablation suppresses refusal on harmful inputs and addition induces it on benign ones, a result underlying subsequent jailbreak and defense methods.

Wollschläger et al. (2025) use gradient-based representation engineering to show that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones, infinite families of directions each capable of mediating refusal, and that identifying genuinely distinct mechanisms requires accounting for linear and nonlinear effects. Zhao et al. (2025) extract a harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a refusal direction at the post-instruction token and show causally that they are separable: models can retain an internal judgment of harmfulness under jailbreaks that suppress refusal outputs.

## Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

### F.1 Limitations

All perturbations rely on Google Translate, whose quality varies widely across language pairs; systematic errors may confound results, particularly under transliteration. WildGuard is the sole primary judge, with NLLB-200 back-translation for non-English responses; back-translation quality degrades for very-low-resource languages and may bias Tier-4 ASR estimates. The geometric analysis is limited to linear probes and mean-difference refusal directions and may miss nonlinear safety mechanisms. Only 8B-scale models are evaluated; whether the tier gradients, script-conditioned bimodality, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal hold at larger scale is open. Attribution of behavioural patterns to representational mechanisms is correlational; causal verification via activation patching is left to future work.

### F.2 Future Work

Activation and path patching would directly test the language-identification disruption hypothesis for code-switching and localise the layers responsible for subthreshold activation failure. Contrastive activation addition along $b_{0}$ is the only geometry-aware repair expected to generalise cross-lingually; whether boosting harmful-activation projections onto $b_{0}$ remediates Tier-3 failures without collapsing multilingual fluency should be evaluated systematically. The benchmark can be extended to further script families (Ethiopic, further Devanagari languages) and attack types (phonetic perturbation, homoglyph substitution). Finally, the script-family structure of secondary cone directions $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$
calls for analysis identifying the training examples that give rise to these language-cluster-specific refusal sub-circuits.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, where they are expected to remain both helpful and safe across languages, scripts, and user populations. In practice, LLMs behave less reliably in non-English and low-resource language contexts because of disparities in
training data, evaluation coverage, and representational fidelity
(Pava and others, 2025). This produces a language gap: users in
lower-resource language communities may receive weaker safety guarantees than users in
English, and current evaluation frameworks are not designed to surface this disparity
systematically. We argue that studying this gap requires richer benchmarks than
aggregate translated-prompt jailbreak rates, together with tools for relating
output-level behavior to internal model representations.

Multilingual prompting can substantially amplify jailbreak success rates
(Deng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), yet the space of multilingual
manipulations an attacker might use is much broader than direct translation.
Real users and adversaries mix languages within a single utterance, write
non-Latin-script languages in Latin characters, and produce text whose phrasing
bears the statistical fingerprints of machine translation. Each of these practices
alters the input in a different way. Code-switching changes only part of the
sentence, romanization changes the script while keeping the language, and
iterative translation changes the distribution of surface forms while keeping the
script and language. A benchmark that collapses all of these into a single
"translated" condition cannot say whether they interact with safety training in
similar or different ways.

Mechanistic work in English-centric settings has established that refusal can be
mediated by a low-dimensional direction in activation space: ablating this
direction suppresses refusal on harmful requests, and adding it can induce refusal
on benign ones (Arditi et al., 2024). This finding reframes safety as a
geometric property of internal encodings. It also makes it possible to inspect
safety behavior through the lens of model activations, not only through
model outputs. Recent work has shown that refusal among safety-aligned languages
is mediated by a single direction Wang et al. (2025), and that harmful
and harmless prompts are often less cleanly separated in non-English representation
spaces (Wang et al., 2025).

We build on this line of work by focusing on the benchmark side of the problem and
on a broad set of representational diagnostics. Rather than re-establishing the
universality of refusal directions, we provide a controlled stress suite of
meaning-preserving perturbations beyond standard translation, encompassing
code-switching, transliteration, and translationese across 18 languages and 4
resource tiers. Because each harmful prompt is paired with a structurally matched
harmless counterpart, the same pairs support both behavioral measurement and
contrastive activation analysis. Behavioral and geometric measurements can
therefore be read side by side for every language and perturbation type.

Several design considerations shaped the benchmark. First, comparisons across
perturbation types are only meaningful if the underlying semantic content is fixed,
so every attack type is applied to the same 385 prompt pairs. Second, comparisons
across languages require a consistent notion of resource level, so we organize
languages into four tiers that span high-resource European and East Asian languages
through to low-resource African and Indigenous American languages. Third, output
evaluation in non-English languages is itself unreliable, so we combine coherence
filtering with back-translation before applying an English-language safety judge.
Finally, mechanistic analyses require consistent token positions and paired inputs,
which our construction provides.

Our contributions are as follows:

1.

We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark
spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated
perturbation types, with harmful-harmless prompt pairs enabling per-attack-type
analysis that prior translation-only benchmarks do not support.

2.

We present an evaluation pipeline and a behavioral study across three
instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and
Aya-Expanse-8B), reporting attack success rates by language, tier, and
perturbation type alongside coherence and safety-regime summaries.

3.

We provide a set of geometric diagnostics on the residual stream: probe-based
harmfulness subspaces, an English-derived refusal direction, silhouette
separation, principal angles, and an activation-domain refusal cone with a
cross-lingual independence measure. These diagnostics can be applied uniformly
across languages and perturbation types and form a foundation for future causal
investigation.

## 2 Related Work

##### Multilingual jailbreak benchmarks.

The empirical backbone of the language-safety gap was established by
Deng et al. (2024), who showed that low-resource languages produce unsafe
outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages. Subsequent
benchmarks have tightened evaluation standards (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024) but remain confined to English. More recent work expands
the attack taxonomy: Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) show that fine-tuning
on harmless low-resource data suffices to jailbreak a model, while
Poppi et al. (2025) demonstrate that safety degradation transfers
cross-lingually through only roughly 20% of model parameters. The work most
directly related to ours, Wang et al. (2025), constructs a
14-language translated-prompt dataset and shows that refusal directions transfer
across languages, attributing persistent jailbreaks to insufficient
harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English spaces. Our benchmark,
Minionese, extends this line by treating linguistic manipulation type
(standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) as an
independent variable, enabling per-attack-type analysis that existing
benchmarks do not support.

##### The refusal mechanism.

Arditi et al. (2024) established that refusal is mediated by a single
low-dimensional direction in activation space, providing the geometric basis for
subsequent jailbreak and defense methods. Wollschläger et al. (2025) refine
this picture, showing that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral
concept cones rather than a single direction. Zhao et al. (2025)
study the mechanism further, identifying a harmfulness direction at the
instruction token and a separate refusal direction at the post-instruction token.
We draw on these tools, specifically probes, mean-difference directions, and
concept cones, and apply them uniformly across the languages and perturbation types
in our benchmark. See Appendix A for an extended discussion of each thread.

## 3 Minionese: A Granular Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmark

We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark designed to
support attack-type-aware analysis. Existing multilingual benchmarks
treat language identity as the primary variable and restrict their attack surface
to standard translation. Minionese instead holds semantic content
constant and varies the type of linguistic manipulation. This allows behavior and
internal representations to be compared across perturbation types on identical
underlying requests.

##### Base corpus.

Minionese is built on the 385 harmful prompts from AdvBench
(Zou et al., 2023). For each harmful prompt, we construct a matched harmless
counterpart by replacing harmful phrases with semantically parallel benign
substitutes using ChatGPT’s GPT-5.4, producing 385 harmful-harmless prompt pairs. Human reviewers
checked each harmless prompt to confirm that sentence structure and length were
preserved, so that surface-level features cannot be used to distinguish
harmful from harmless inputs at the token level. Matched pairs of this kind are
standard in contrastive activation work. They ensure that differences between the
harmful and harmless activation sets reflect the content substitution, not
incidental differences in length or syntax.

##### Languages and resource tiers.

The benchmark spans 18 languages grouped into four resource tiers based on
training-data availability in contemporary LLMs:

•

Tier 1 (high-resource): English, Spanish, Chinese, German,
French

•

Tier 2 (mid-high resource): Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese

•

Tier 3 (mid-low resource): Turkish, Indonesian, Hindi, Swahili

•

Tier 4 (low-resource): Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní,
Javanese

The tiering is a pragmatic grouping, not a precise measure of pretraining
exposure. Exact data proportions for the evaluated models are not public, and
availability of instruction-tuning and safety data may differ from availability of
raw pretraining text. The tiers nonetheless provide a convenient axis for
organizing results. The language set also spans a variety of scripts (Latin,
Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari, Hangul, Han characters, and Japanese kana), which is
essential for the transliteration condition.

All translations are produced using the Google Translate API. Each of the four
attack types below is applied to every harmful-harmless pair across all 18
languages, yielding a benchmark of $385\times 2\times 4\times 18=55,440$
total prompts. Examples of each attack type are listed in Section E of the appendix.

### 3.1 Attack Types

##### Standard translation.

Each harmful-harmless prompt pair is translated in full to the target language.
This attack type serves as the baseline condition and replicates the setting of
prior multilingual jailbreak studies.

##### Code-switching.

Code-switching targets the minimal span that distinguishes the harmful prompt from
its harmless counterpart. We tokenize each pair into words and punctuation marks,
identify the contiguous differing span, and translate only the alphabetic tokens
within that span into the target language. All shared context outside the
differing span remains in English. This construction mirrors a common pattern in
naturally occurring bilingual text, where content words are inserted from one
language into a frame provided by another. It also lets us isolate the effect of
expressing only the semantically critical span in another language.

##### Transliteration.

Transliteration converts a fully translated prompt into a phonetic rendering in a
different script, preserving pronunciation while discarding native orthography.
We first translate each prompt into the target language, then apply script
conversion: prompts in non-Romance languages are converted to Latin characters
(Romanization), while prompts in Romance languages are converted to a Latin-Cyrillic
rendering. This perturbation is designed to stress-test refusal mechanisms that
operate on script or token identity rather than semantic content. Romanized text
is widespread in informal online communication for languages such as Hindi,
Arabic, and Chinese, which makes this a realistic as well as a controlled
manipulation.

##### Translationese.

Translationese introduces semantic drift by applying iterative round-trip
translation. The original English prompt is translated to the target language,
back-translated to English, and translated to the target language once more, for
three translation steps in total. The final
prompt retains the target language but carries the surface statistics of machine-
translated text, testing whether refusal mechanisms are sensitive to these
distributional features.

## 4 Evaluation

We evaluate three models across all 18 languages and 4 perturbation types in
Minionese, measuring attack success rate (ASR), response coherence, and
safety regime distribution. The evaluation pipeline proceeds in three stages:
response generation, coherence filtering, and safety scoring via back-translated
WildGuard judgments.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### 4.1.1 Models and Inference

We evaluate three instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Aya-Expanse-8B. All models are run with greedy decoding (temperature $=0$ ) and a maximum of 512 new tokens. The three models were chosen because they are comparable in scale but differ in their multilingual training emphasis. Aya-Expanse is explicitly designed for broad multilingual coverage, Qwen has strong coverage of Chinese and other Asian languages, and Llama is a widely used general-purpose baseline. Greedy decoding makes the evaluation deterministic and simplifies comparison across conditions.

#### 4.1.2 Coherence Filtering

For each (model, language, perturbation) triple, we generate responses for all
385 harmful and 385 harmless prompt pairs. Because multilingual failures often
co-occur with degraded generation quality, each response is assessed for
coherence via language identification (langdetect) and Unicode
validity. A response is marked incoherent if any of the following conditions
hold: (i) its detected language matches neither the target language nor English;
(ii) language identification confidence falls below 0.3; (iii) Unicode validity
falls below 0.8; or (iv) response length is under 20 characters. Incoherent
responses are excluded from ASR computation. Coherence rates are uniformly at or
near 1.0 across all conditions, indicating that the filter removes very few
responses and that the evaluated outputs are well-formed text.

#### 4.1.3 Attack Success Rate Measurement

We measure ASR using WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) as the
primary safety judge. For non-English responses, we back-translate to English prior to scoring, to
mitigate WildGuard’s reduced reliability on non-English text. A response is
counted as an attack success if WildGuard does not classify it as a refusal. ASR
is computed as the fraction of harmful prompts eliciting compliant responses
within each (language, perturbation, model) cell:

| | $\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{model}(x)\ \text{is compliant}\right],$
| | (1)

where $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}$ denotes the set of harmful prompts and
$\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function. We report ASR per language, per
perturbation type, and aggregated by resource tier. We additionally report
$\Delta$ ASR relative to the English baseline to quantify per-condition
change relative to the model’s English behavior.

Back-translation followed by English-language judging is a pragmatic compromise.
Safety classifiers trained mainly on English data are known to behave
inconsistently on other languages, and multilingual safety judges with
comparable calibration are not yet widely available. Back-translation can itself
introduce noise, particularly for lower-resource languages, and we return to this
issue in Appendix F.

### 4.2 Results

Figure 1: ASR by language and perturbation type, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Heatmaps for
Aya and Qwen are in Appendix B.

Per-language, per-attack-type ASR heatmaps are shown in
Figure 1 (Llama); the corresponding heatmaps for Qwen and Aya are
given in Appendix B. The heatmaps are organized with languages along one axis,
grouped by tier, and perturbation types along the other. This layout allows
variation along each axis to be inspected directly.

#### 4.2.1 Attack Type and Tier Profiles

##### Standard translation and translationese follow a tier gradient.

Standard translation and translationese are the two conditions in which the entire
prompt is rendered in the target language in its native script. Their ASR is
therefore most naturally organized by resource tier, and Figure 1
presents them in tier order for direct comparison. The two conditions differ only
in the additional round-trip steps applied in translationese, so any difference
between them in a given language reflects how sensitive the model is to
machine-translation surface statistics as opposed to the language itself.
Prior work has largely studied standard translation alone (Deng et al., 2024;
Wang et al., 2025). Including translationese gives a second, closely related
condition against which the standard-translation baseline can be checked.

##### Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned.

Transliteration changes the script of the prompt while preserving its
pronunciation, and its effect cannot be read independently of the native script of
each language. For non-Latin-script languages, romanization replaces the native
orthography with Latin characters. For Latin-script languages, the
Latin-Cyrillic rendering instead moves the prompt into an unfamiliar script. The
transliteration column of Figure 1 and its counterparts in
Appendix B should therefore be read with each language's native script in mind, not
in tier order alone. Because $\Delta$ ASR is reported relative to English, the
same column can also indicate conditions in which transliterated prompts are
handled differently from the English baseline.

##### Code-switching produces the most tier-stable attack profile.

Code-switching differs from the other conditions in that most of each prompt
remains in English and only the minimal differing span is translated. The
manipulation is thus confined to the content words that carry the harmful or
benign meaning, while the instruction frame is unchanged. This makes the
code-switching column a useful contrast with standard translation. The two
conditions express the same semantically critical words in the same target
language but embed them in different surrounding contexts.

##### The safety regime transitions sharply between Tiers 2 and 3.

Beyond ASR, we summarize each (model, tier) cell by the distribution of responses
across refusing, complying, and mixed regimes. This view complements the
per-language ASR heatmaps by aggregating over languages within a tier and over
prompts within a language. It is useful for distinguishing conditions in which
behavior is uniform across prompts from conditions in which models respond
inconsistently. The regime summaries are reported per model, since the three models
differ in their multilingual training emphasis and the boundaries between regimes
need not coincide across architectures.

#### 4.2.2 Cross-Model Consistency

Evaluating three models with different multilingual training regimes allows us to
ask which features of the ASR profiles are shared and which are model-specific.
The heatmaps in Figure 1 and Appendix B use identical language and
perturbation orderings to facilitate this comparison. Shared structure across
architectures would point toward properties of the perturbations or of safety
alignment in general. Divergences would point toward differences in training data
or alignment procedures. Absolute ASR levels are also of interest in their own
right, since they indicate how much each model's English safety behavior carries
over to the other languages and perturbations in the benchmark.

## 5 Geometric Analysis of Refusal

We complement the behavioral evaluation with a set of geometric diagnostics on
residual-stream activations. The aim of this section is descriptive: to provide
layer-wise, per-language measurements of how harmful and harmless prompts are
represented and how these representations relate to a refusal direction extracted
from English. We use linear probing, subspace construction, and cross-lingual
comparison, applying each tool uniformly across languages so that measurements are
directly comparable.

### 5.1 Preliminaries

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with $L$ layers and hidden dimension $d$ . We
extract residual stream activations $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at the last post-instruction token position $t^{*}$ for each input
$\mathbf{x}$ . For language $\lambda$ and layer $\ell$ , we define harmful and
harmless activation sets $\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ and
$\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ from our paired benchmark.

##### Harmfulness subspace.

For each $(\lambda,\ell)$ , we train a logistic regression probe and stack weights
across harm categories into $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{C}|}$ , where $\mathcal{C}$ is comprised of “all “ and “unknown” categories derived from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). The harmfulness subspace $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ is the
column space of the top- $k$ right singular vectors of
$\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , with $k$ selected to explain $\geq 95\%$ of
spectral mass.

##### Refusal direction.

We extract $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ from English activations
via behavioral contrast between refused ( $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}$ ) and complied
( $\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}$ ) sets:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}\|_{2}}$
| | (2)

This is the standard difference-in-means construction used in prior refusal work
(Arditi et al., 2024), and it is extracted from English only so that it can
serve as a fixed reference against which activations from all other languages are
measured.

##### Failure classification.

Following Zhao et al. (2025), we also compute, for each
$(\lambda,\ell)$ pair, components of the activation associated with the
harmfulness subspace and with the refusal direction, and record their norms and
contrastive signals. These quantities are reported as per-language, per-layer
summaries in Appendix C. We additionally record the projection
$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)\top}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})$ of each activation
onto the refusal direction and compare it against a reference level
$\tau^{(\ell)}=0.95$ , which gives a uniform scale on which conditions can be
compared. We treat these summaries as descriptive measurements of the residual
stream, without assigning a causal interpretation to them in the present study.

### 5.2 Results

Figure 2: Harmful-harmless separation in activation space (silhouette score)
across languages and layers, all three models using standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmful-harmless separation degrades with resource tier.

Figure 2 reports silhouette scores (Rousseeuw, 1987)
in the harmfulness-subspace-projected residual stream for every language and layer,
using the standard-translation condition. The silhouette score summarizes how
tightly harmful and harmless activations cluster relative to the distance between
the two clusters, and it is bounded in $[-1,1]$ . Plotting it across layers shows
at what depth separation emerges and whether it persists through the network. The
figure is organized by tier so that per-language curves can be compared against one
another and against the corresponding ASR values in Section 4.2.

Because the projection is onto a language-specific harmfulness subspace, the
silhouette score measures separation within each language's own representation,
not relative to English. It therefore complements the cross-lingual subspace
comparison reported below.

Figure 3: Linear probe AUC for harmfulness detection across all layers using standard_translation attack type
(category all; chance $=0.5$ ).

##### Probe AUC confirms subthreshold activation as the dominant failure mode.

Figure 3 shows 5-fold cross-validated probe AUC across the
full layer range for every language under standard translation. AUC measures
whether harmful and harmless prompts are linearly distinguishable from a single
layer's activations, independent of the threshold a downstream classifier might
use. It is therefore a less geometry-dependent summary than the silhouette score.
Reading the probe curves alongside the ASR heatmaps allows one to compare, for each
language, how decodable harmfulness is in the residual stream with how often the
model complies with harmful requests.

Linear probes have well-known limitations as evidence about model computation
(Appendix F). High probe accuracy shows that information is linearly
present, not that the model uses that information for any downstream decision. We
therefore report AUC as a representational measurement that complements, and does
not substitute for, the behavioral evaluation.

Figure 4: Principal angle between non-English and English safety subspaces as a
function of normalized layer depth, per tier and model for standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmfulness subspaces are not cross-lingually universal.

Figure 4 shows the first principal angle
$\theta^{(\ell)}_{\lambda,1}$ between non-English and English harmfulness
subspaces as a function of normalized layer depth, aggregated by tier for each
model. Principal angles provide a basis-independent measure of the geometric
relationship between two subspaces. An angle of $0^{\circ}$ indicates that the
subspaces share a direction, and $90^{\circ}$ indicates that they are orthogonal.
Normalizing depth allows the three models, which differ in layer count, to be
plotted on a common axis.

The comparison is directly relevant to the use of an English-derived refusal
direction. Prior work showing cross-lingual transfer of refusal directions
(Wang et al., 2025) motivates asking how harmfulness representations in
other languages relate geometrically to their English counterparts. Figure
4 provides this measurement for every tier and model.

##### Harm and refusal signals are geometrically decoupled.

Figure 9 (Appendix C) presents four
complementary views of the harm and refusal components defined in Section
5.1 across all three models. The first row plots harm and refusal
component norms per language. The second plots the per-language contrastive harm
signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{harm}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{inst}}$ against the refusal signal
$\sigma_{\mathrm{refusal}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{post}}$ . The third reports the layer-wise
distribution of component summaries per language. The fourth shows tier-averaged
harm and refusal signal trajectories across normalized layer depth. Together these
views allow the two components to be inspected jointly, language by language and
layer by layer. Measuring the harm signal at the instruction token and the refusal
signal at the post-instruction token follows the token-position conventions of
Zhao et al. (2025).

These summaries are intended as a resource for further investigation. Whether the
relationships they display generalize beyond the three 8B-scale models studied
here, and whether they carry causal significance, are questions we leave to future
work with intervention-based methods.

##### Synthesis.

The diagnostics in this section are complementary views of the same paired
activations. Silhouette scores describe within-language clustering, probe AUC
describes linear decodability, principal angles describe cross-lingual subspace
geometry, and the component summaries in Appendix C describe the relationship
between harmfulness-related and refusal-related signals. Because all of them are
computed on the matched harmful–harmless pairs of Minionese at a common
token position, they can be read side by side, and alongside the behavioral results
of Section 4.2, for any language of interest. We emphasize that these
are correlational measurements. Establishing which representational properties are
responsible for particular behavioral outcomes requires causal methods such as
activation patching, which we discuss in Appendix F.

### 5.3 Refusal Cone Structure and Cross-Lingual Representational Independence

The prior analyses use a single mean-difference direction $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ .
Wollschläger et al. (2025) show for English-centric settings that refusal is
governed by multi-dimensional concept cones. We extend this framework to
the multilingual domain with two contributions: (i) activation-domain cone
optimisation, fitting the cone basis directly on cached residual activations
rather than via gradient-based model interventions; and (ii) Cross-Lingual
Representational Independence (CL-RepInd), which measures whether two refusal
basis directions exploit shared or distinct cross-lingual circuits.

##### Cone optimisation.

Let $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ be an orthonormal basis for an
$N$ -dimensional refusal cone, seeded with $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ . We optimise
$\mathbf{B}$ to maximise the harmful–harmless margin along each basis direction
on English activations while penalising directions whose margin collapses on
non-English activations:

| | $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})=&-\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})}_{\text{EN margin}}+\lambda_{\rm cone}\underbrace{\vphantom{\frac{1}{N}}\bigl({\rm ReLU}(\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})-\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i-1}))\bigr)}_{\text{cone spread}}\\
&-\lambda_{\rm xl}\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\Delta_{\lambda}(b_{i})}_{\text{CL margin}},\end{split}$
| | (3)

where $\Delta_{\lambda}(b)$ is the harmful–harmless margin along $b$ for language
$\lambda$ and $\Lambda$ is the set of non-English languages. We use Stiefel-manifold
gradient ascent for 400 steps ( $\eta\!=\!0.05$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{cone}}\!=\!5$ ,
$\lambda_{\mathrm{xl}}\!=\!1$ ), fitting $N\!\in\!\{1,\ldots,5\}$ and treating
$N\!=\!5$ as canonical. CL-RepInd is the Pearson correlation of the per-language
margin vectors for two basis directions; low correlation indicates they exploit
different cross-lingual circuits.

Fitting the cone in the activation domain has practical advantages. It requires
only cached activations, which avoids repeated forward passes with interventions,
and it allows the English and cross-lingual objectives to be traded off explicitly
through $\lambda_{\mathrm{xl}}$ . The Stiefel-manifold parameterization keeps the
basis orthonormal throughout optimization, so margins along different basis
directions measure distinct directions in activation space.

##### Results (Figures 5–6,
Appendix D).

Figure 5 reports cone quality as a function of dimensionality
$N$ , together with English and cross-lingual margins for each direction of the
canonical $N\!=\!5$ basis, for Aya and Qwen. Figure 6 breaks the
cross-lingual margins down by language, with tier boundaries marked so that
per-language margins can be compared within and across tiers. The corresponding
figures for Llama are given in Appendix D. CL-RepInd is computed for every pair of
basis directions and summarizes whether the per-language margin profiles of
different directions co-vary. Taken together, these figures characterize how the
English refusal cone fitted on each model relates to the activations of the other
17 languages in the benchmark.

The cone framework generalizes the single-direction analysis. When $N\!=\!1$ the
basis consists of the seed direction alone, so the progression from $N\!=\!1$ to
$N\!=\!5$ shows how much additional structure is captured by higher-dimensional
refusal representations in each model.

## 6 Discussion

Minionese is designed to make multilingual safety evaluation more
granular. Treating perturbation type as an independent variable makes it possible to ask
questions that translation-only benchmarks cannot pose: whether code-switched
prompts behave like fully translated ones, whether romanized prompts behave like
their native-script counterparts, and whether machine-translation surface
statistics matter independently of language. The matched harmful–harmless
construction extends the same granularity to activation space. Every behavioral
condition has a corresponding contrastive activation set that can be analyzed with
the same tools.

##### Refusal geometry is effectively one-dimensional cross-lingually.

The refusal cone analysis (Section 5.3) connects our
multilingual setting to the multi-dimensional picture of refusal proposed by
Wollschläger et al. (2025). In English-centric work, the existence of
multiple refusal directions raises the question of whether these directions encode
redundant or distinct mechanisms. In a multilingual setting the question gains an
additional dimension: whether the directions that mediate refusal in English play a
comparable role for other languages. The CL-RepInd measure is intended to make this
question quantitative, and the per-language margin heatmaps provide the raw material
for answering it on a language-by-language basis. Geometry-aware safety
interventions such as contrastive activation addition and refusal subspace
projection are increasingly proposed as lightweight defenses. Measurements of this
kind are a natural prerequisite for deciding how such interventions should be
applied in multilingual deployments.

##### Tier-4 failure is upstream, not directional.

The lowest-resource tier deserves particular attention in any multilingual safety
study. Tier-4 languages in Minionese, including Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish
Gaelic, Guaraní, and Javanese, are spoken by large communities but are sparsely
represented in pretraining and alignment corpora. They are also the languages for
which translation and back-translation quality is hardest to guarantee. Behavioral
and representational measurements for these languages should therefore be
interpreted together and with caution, and the per-language breakdowns we provide
are intended to support exactly this kind of careful reading. Within-tier variation
is also informative: resource tier is a coarse grouping, and individual languages
may depart from the typical profile of their tier for reasons related to script,
typology, or the composition of particular training corpora.

##### Cross-model consistency.

The three models we evaluate differ substantially in their multilingual training.
Aya-Expanse targets broad language coverage, Qwen emphasizes Chinese and other
Asian languages, and Llama is a general-purpose model with comparatively less
explicit multilingual focus. Comparing behavioral and geometric measurements across
these architectures helps separate properties of the benchmark perturbations from
properties of particular training pipelines. A broader model sample, including
larger models and models from additional families, would strengthen any such
comparison. Extended limitations and future work directions are in Appendix F.

## 7 Conclusion

We introduced Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18
languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types,
and evaluated it across three instruction-tuned models. The benchmark holds
semantic content fixed across 385 matched harmful–harmless prompt pairs and varies
the type of linguistic manipulation, including standard translation, code-switching,
transliteration, and translationese. This supports evaluation broken down by
language, tier, and perturbation type, and it goes beyond the translation-only
setting of prior multilingual benchmarks.

Alongside the benchmark, we presented an evaluation pipeline that combines
coherence filtering with back-translated WildGuard judgments, and a suite of
geometric diagnostics applied uniformly across languages: probe-based harmfulness
subspaces, an English-derived refusal direction, silhouette separation, principal
angles between harmfulness subspaces, harm and refusal component summaries, and an
activation-domain refusal cone with a cross-lingual representational independence
measure. These tools allow behavioral outcomes and internal representations to be
examined side by side for every condition in the benchmark.

The refusal cone construction contributes two methodological elements: fitting the
cone directly on cached activations with an explicit cross-lingual term, and
measuring whether distinct cone directions share cross-lingual margin profiles.
Both are inexpensive to compute and can be applied to any model for which residual
activations are available.

We hope Minionese will serve as a resource for multilingual red-teaming,
for the design of evaluation protocols that account for script family and
perturbation type, and for causal studies of how safety behavior is
implemented across languages. Safety evaluation that is responsive to the full
range of languages and linguistic practices of real users is an important
component of responsible global deployment.

## Impact Statement

This paper aims to improve the safety and equity of multilingual LLM deployment by providing tools for examining how models respond to harmful prompts in lower-resource languages and under perturbations such as transliteration, code-switching, and translationese. By introducing Minionese and a set of representational diagnostics, we provide resources for multilingual safety evaluation, red-teaming, and future alignment interventions. While this work could make vulnerable language–attack combinations more accessible, we mitigate this risk by emphasizing evaluation and measurement rather than optimized attack recipes or harmful completions. Overall, we believe that broad multilingual measurement is necessary for responsible deployment, since evaluation concentrated on a single language can obscure risks faced by non-English and low-resource language communities.

## Appendix A Extended Related Work

### A.1 Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmarks and the Low-Resource Safety Gap

The fragility of LLM safety alignment across languages was first systematically
characterized by Deng et al. (2024), who demonstrated that low-resource
languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource
languages across both unintentional and intentional jailbreak scenarios. Their
benchmark, MultiJail, establishes the empirical backbone of the language-safety
gap, though its attack surface is restricted to standard translation. On the
English side, Zou et al. (2023) provide AdvBench, the foundational
benchmark of harmful behaviors that subsequent multilingual studies build upon;
their greedy-gradient suffix attack further underscores that aligned models remain
adversarially brittle in their primary training language. Chao et al. (2024)
address reproducibility issues in jailbreak evaluation with a standardized,
open-sourced benchmark and unified threat model, though it too is English-only.
These resources establish rigorous evaluation standards but leave the multilingual
dimension underspecified.

More recent work has expanded the attack taxonomy. Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025)
demonstrate that fine-tuning an LLM on entirely harmless data in a new,
low-resource language is sufficient to jailbreak the model. They attribute the
effect to late-layer pivots that override safety-critical representations with
language-fidelity objectives. Poppi et al. (2025) show
that fine-tuning attacks generalize cross-lingually: compromising a model in one
language degrades its safety in others, with only approximately 20% of weight
parameters implicated, suggesting that safety information is largely
language-agnostic at the parameter level.

Wang et al. (2025), the work most directly related to ours,
construct a 14-language dataset of translated harmful prompts and demonstrate that
refusal directions extracted from English transfer with near-perfect effectiveness
to other languages, with refusal vectors approximately parallel in activation
space. They further identify that insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation
in non-English languages explains why cross-lingual jailbreaks persist even when a
universal refusal direction is present.

Our work departs from this line in one important respect. Rather than treating
language identity as the sole independent variable, Minionese
systematically varies the type of linguistic manipulation (standard translation,
code-switching, transliteration, and translationese) while holding semantic
content constant. This enables a per-attack-type analysis that neither
MultiJail nor PolyRefuse supports. It also broadens the attack surface to include
manipulations that occur naturally in multilingual online communication, such as
mixing languages within an utterance and writing languages in a non-native script.

### A.2 The Refusal Mechanism in Large Language Models

Mechanistic understanding of refusal has advanced rapidly through the framework of
linear representation engineering. Arditi et al. (2024) established that
refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction
in activation space: ablating this direction suppresses refusal on harmful inputs,
and adding it induces refusal on benign ones. This result, initially demonstrated
in English, provides the geometric basis for the jailbreak and defense methods that
follow.

Subsequent work has complicated and enriched this picture.
Wollschläger et al. (2025) challenge the single-direction assumption,
showing through gradient-based representation engineering that refusal is governed
by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones, infinite families of directions all
capable of mediating refusal, and that accounting for both linear and nonlinear
effects is necessary to identify genuinely distinct mechanisms.
Zhao et al. (2025) push the analysis further, extracting a
harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a refusal direction at the
post-instruction token, and studying how the two relate under jailbreaks.

These works share a methodological core that we adopt: contrastive activation
sets, linear directions or subspaces fitted to those sets, and measurements of how
new inputs project onto the fitted geometry. Our contribution on this front is to
apply these tools consistently across a much broader set of languages and
perturbations than the English-centric settings in which they were developed, and
to introduce an activation-domain cone fitting procedure and a cross-lingual
independence measure suited to the multilingual case.
