## 2 Related Work

##### Multilingual jailbreak benchmarks.

Deng et al. (2024) showed that low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages. Subsequent benchmarks tightened evaluation standards (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024) but remain English-only. Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) show that fine-tuning on harmless low-resource data suffices to jailbreak a model, and Poppi et al. (2025) demonstrate that safety degradation transfers cross-lingually through only roughly 20% of model parameters. Wang et al. (2025) construct a 14-language translated-prompt dataset, show that refusal directions transfer across languages, and attribute persistent jailbreaks to insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English spaces. Minionese treats linguistic manipulation type (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) as an independent variable, which existing benchmarks do not.

##### The refusal mechanism.

Arditi et al. (2024) established that refusal is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction in activation space. Wollschläger et al. (2025) show that refusal is instead governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones. Zhao et al. (2025) identify a harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a separate refusal direction at the post-instruction token, with causal evidence that the two dissociate under jailbreaks. We carry the harmfulness detection / refusal activation distinction into the multilingual domain. See Appendix A for an extended discussion of each thread.

## 3 Minionese: A Granular Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmark

Existing multilingual benchmarks take language identity as the primary variable and restrict the attack surface to standard translation. Minionese holds semantic content constant and varies the type of linguistic manipulation.

##### Base corpus.

Minionese is built on the 385 harmful prompts from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023). For each harmful prompt, a matched harmless counterpart is constructed by replacing harmful phrases with semantically parallel benign substitutes using ChatGPT’s GPT-5.4, producing 385 harmful-harmless prompt pairs. Human reviewers verified that every harmless prompt preserves the sentence structure and length of its harmful counterpart, so that surface-level features cannot distinguish harmful from harmless inputs at the token level.

##### Languages and resource tiers.

The benchmark spans 18 languages grouped into four resource tiers by training-data availability in contemporary LLMs:

•

Tier 1 (high-resource): English, Spanish, Chinese, German,
French

•

Tier 2 (mid-high resource): Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese

•

Tier 3 (mid-low resource): Turkish, Indonesian, Hindi, Swahili

•

Tier 4 (low-resource): Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní,
Javanese

All translations use the Google Translate API. Each of the four attack types is applied to every harmful-harmless pair in all 18 languages, yielding $385\times 2\times 4\times 18=55,440$ total prompts. Examples of each attack type are listed in Section E of the appendix.

### 3.1 Attack Types

##### Standard translation.

Each harmful-harmless prompt pair is translated in full into the target language, replicating the setting of prior multilingual jailbreak studies; this is the baseline condition.

##### Code-switching.

Each pair is tokenized into words and punctuation marks, the contiguous span on which the harmful and harmless prompts differ is identified, and only the alphabetic tokens within that span are translated into the target language. All shared context outside the differing span remains in English.

##### Transliteration.

Each prompt is first translated into the target language and then script-converted: non-Romance languages are rendered in Latin characters (Romanization), and Romance languages in a Latin-Cyrillic rendering. Pronunciation is preserved while native orthography is discarded, stress-testing refusal mechanisms that key on script or token identity rather than semantic content.

##### Translationese.

The English prompt is translated into the target language, back-translated to English, and translated into the target language once more, for three translation steps in total. The final prompt is in the target language but carries the surface statistics of machine-translated text.

## 4 Evaluation

Three models are evaluated across all 18 languages and 4 perturbation types for attack success rate (ASR), response coherence, and safety regime distribution, via response generation, coherence filtering, and safety scoring with back-translated WildGuard judgments.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### 4.1.1 Models and Inference

We evaluate three instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Aya-Expanse-8B. All models are run with greedy decoding (temperature $=0$ ) and a maximum of 512 new tokens.

#### 4.1.2 Coherence Filtering

For each (model, language, perturbation) triple, responses are generated for all 385 harmful and 385 harmless prompts and assessed for coherence via language identification (langdetect) and Unicode validity. A response is marked incoherent if (i) its detected language matches neither the target language nor English; (ii) language identification confidence falls below 0.3; (iii) Unicode validity falls below 0.8; or (iv) response length is under 20 characters. Incoherent responses are excluded from ASR computation. Coherence rates are uniformly at or near 1.0 across all conditions (see Section 4.2).

#### 4.1.3 Attack Success Rate Measurement

WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) is the primary safety judge. Non-English responses are back-translated to English prior to scoring to mitigate WildGuard’s reduced reliability on non-English text. A response counts as an attack success if WildGuard does not classify it as a refusal. ASR is the fraction of harmful prompts eliciting compliant responses within each (language, perturbation, model) cell:

| | $\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{model}(x)\ \text{is compliant}\right],$
| | (1)

where $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}$ denotes the set of harmful prompts and $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function. ASR is reported per language, per perturbation type, and aggregated by resource tier, together with $\Delta$ ASR relative to the English baseline.

##### Standard translation and translationese follow a tier gradient.

For both attack types, ASR increases substantially with decreasing resource level on all three models. Under standard translation, Llama mean ASR rises from approximately 8% in Tier 1 to over 70% in Tiers 3–4 (Yoruba 100%, Zulu 97%, Scottish Gaelic 98%). Qwen follows suit (Swahili 96%, Scottish Gaelic 90%, Yoruba 75%); Aya shows a more moderate gradient except at Swahili, which reaches 95%. Translationese consistently exceeds standard translation ASR at mid-resource languages, with the largest gaps for Korean (14% vs. 51% on Aya) and Hindi (15% vs. 48% on Llama), in line with round-trip translation shifting phrasing toward naturalistic surface forms that weaken harmfulness detection upstream of refusal.

##### Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned.

Transliteration yields the highest ASR of any attack type for non-Latin-script languages in Tiers 1–2: Korean 98% on Aya and 99% on Llama; Chinese 97% on Llama; Arabic 84% on Aya; Hindi 99% on Llama. For Latin-script and very-low-resource Tier-4 languages, transliteration ASR drops to near zero (French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on both Aya and Qwen). On Qwen, $\Delta$ ASR is negative for Yoruba ( $-38\%$ ), Russian ( $-48\%$ ), and Scottish Gaelic ( $-44\%$ ), i.e. romanized inputs in these languages are rejected more robustly than the English baseline. The bimodality replicates across all three models.

##### Code-switching produces the most tier-stable attack profile.

Code-switching maintains moderate-to-high ASR across all resource tiers and models. Tier-4 languages show elevated code-switching ASR even where other attack types are near zero: Yoruba (62% on Aya, 82% on Llama), Zulu (62% on Aya, 85% on Llama), and Guaraní (42% on Aya, 46% on Llama). The tier gradient is present but substantially shallower than under standard translation, consistent with disrupted language-identification routing rather than degraded semantic representation.

##### The safety regime transitions sharply between Tiers 2 and 3.

All three models predominantly refuse in Tiers 1–2: Llama 80% refuse in Tier 1 and 75% in Tier 2; Qwen 80% and 88%; Aya 75% in both. At Tier 3, Llama drops to 31% refuse, Qwen to 50%, and Aya to 31%, with Aya reaching 95% comply by Tier 4. A mixed regime is nearly absent across all models and tiers: language-perturbation combinations produce coherent behavioral modes rather than uncertain outputs, pointing to a threshold effect in refusal activation rather than continuous degradation.

#### 4.2.2 Cross-Model Consistency

Qualitative profiles agree across models while absolute magnitudes diverge substantially. The rank ordering of attack types by mean ASR is stable: transliteration dominates for Tier-1 and Tier-2 non-Latin-script languages, code-switching dominates at Tier 4, and standard translation and translationese form the closest-matched and generally lowest-ASR pair, suggesting structural properties of transformer safety circuits rather than model-specific training artifacts.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is the most broadly vulnerable model, with Tier-4 standard translation mean ASR approaching 80%, against approximately 55% for Qwen and 35% for Aya. The script-conditioned bimodality in transliteration reproduces across all three architectures (Appendix B), locating it in the romanization operation itself.

## 5 Geometric Analysis of Refusal

Multilingual jailbreak vulnerability is analyzed as a two-stage representational failure, with harmful content either undetected upstream or detected but failing to activate refusal downstream, operationalized through linear probing, subspace construction, and cross-lingual transfer analysis.

### 5.1 Preliminaries

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with $L$ layers and hidden dimension $d$ . We extract residual stream activations $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at the last post-instruction token position $t^{*}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$ . For language $\lambda$ and layer $\ell$ , harmful and harmless activation sets $\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ and $\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ are taken from the paired benchmark.

##### Harmfulness subspace.

For each $(\lambda,\ell)$ , we train a logistic regression probe and stack weights across harm categories into $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{C}|}$ , where $\mathcal{C}$ is comprised of “all “ and “unknown” categories derived from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). The harmfulness subspace $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ is the column space of the top- $k$ right singular vectors of $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , with $k$ selected to explain $\geq 95\%$ of spectral mass.

##### Refusal direction.

$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is extracted from English activations by behavioral contrast between refused ( $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}$ ) and complied ( $\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}$ ) sets:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}\|_{2}}$
| | (2)

##### Failure classification.

Following Zhao et al. (2025), harm and refusal components are disentangled and each $(\lambda,\ell)$ pair is labeled upstream, downstream, or mixed. Refusal is modeled as the threshold decision $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)\top}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})>\tau^{(\ell)}$ , and a language exhibits subthreshold activation when harmful activations fail to exceed $\tau^{(\ell)}=0.95$ despite nontrivial harm signal.

### 5.2 Results

##### Harmful-harmless separation degrades with resource tier.

Figure 2 reports silhouette scores (Rousseeuw, 1987) in the harmfulness-subspace-projected residual stream. Tier-1 and Tier-2 languages maintain high, stable separation across the full layer range on all three models. Separation declines from Tier 3 onward, consistently across architectures. Guaraní (gn) reaches near-zero and negative silhouette scores across all layers on all models, the sharpest representational degeneration in the benchmark. Swahili (sw) scores substantially below other Tier-3 languages on all three models, matching its anomalously high ASR (Section 4.2).

The tier ordering is fixed by mid-network depth and remains stable thereafter; later layers do not recover separation for lower-resource languages, so representational quality is set at encoding rather than by depth-specific processing. The absolute Tier-1-to-Tier-4 gap is consistent across architectures, largest for Aya.

##### Probe AUC confirms subthreshold activation as the dominant failure mode.

Figure 3 shows 5-fold cross-validated probe AUC across the full layer range. All three models attain high AUC ( ${\geq}0.85$ ) from early layers onward for Tiers 1–3; degradation is concentrated in Tier-4 languages, with Yoruba and Zulu approaching chance in late layers across all models. Harmfulness is thus linearly decodable in the residual stream for all but the very lowest-resource languages.

For Tier-3 languages, probe AUC remains high in language-perturbation conditions with elevated ASR, the signature of subthreshold activation failure. For Tier-4 languages, AUC degradation toward chance is consistent with semantic recovery failure.

Figure 4: Principal angle between non-English and English safety subspaces as a
function of normalized layer depth, per tier and model for standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmfulness subspaces are not cross-lingually universal.

Figure 4 shows the first principal angle $\theta^{(\ell)}_{\lambda,1}$ between non-English and English harmfulness subspaces against normalized layer depth. No tier approaches $0^{\circ}$ : Tier-1 languages sit at $40$ – $65^{\circ}$ depending on the model, and Tier-4 languages approach near-orthogonality ( ${\sim}85$ – $90^{\circ}$ ) on all three architectures. Angles are broadly stable across depth, ruling out a late-layer cross-lingual alignment of non-English harmfulness subspaces toward English. Qwen exhibits the smallest mean angles ( ${\approx}60$ – $65^{\circ}$ ), in line with its comparatively higher Tier-4 silhouette scores in Figure 2.

A universal refusal direction mediates refusal across languages only insofar as the upstream harmfulness signal projects onto it, and the monotonic increase of principal angles from Tier 1 to Tier 4 tracks the ASR tier gradient.

##### Harm and refusal signals are geometrically decoupled.

Figure 9 (Appendix C) presents four views of the harmfulness-refusal disentanglement across all three models. Harm and refusal component norms are weakly correlated and widely scattered on all three models. Swahili, Scottish Gaelic, Yoruba, and Zulu each have instances across the models with disproportionately large harm norm relative to refusal component, a per-language signature of subthreshold activation. For Aya and Llama, the per-language contrastive harm signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{harm}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{inst}}$ is strongly negatively correlated with the refusal signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{refusal}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{post}}$ : $r=-0.79$ for Aya and $r=-0.68$ for Llama. Qwen instead exhibits a positive correlation, $r=+0.53$ . Whether Tier-4 language clusters occupy the low-harm, variable-refusal region universally across models remains open.

Layer-wise failure classification is predominantly mixed for all three models. A small number of upstream classifications appear in Tier-4 languages. Downstream failure is not observed in any model.

##### Synthesis.

Tier-1 inputs satisfy both prerequisites for reliable refusal: clean harmful-harmless separation and adequate projection onto the refusal direction. For Tier-3–4 inputs, one or both fail. In the dominant mixed mode, a usable harmfulness representation is present at the instruction token but lies in a misaligned, low-rank subspace whose intersection with $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ is insufficient to cross the refusal threshold. In the lowest-resource Tier-4 languages, the harm representation additionally degrades toward chance. Multilingual jailbreaks succeed not by destroying $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ but by starving it of input.

### 5.3 Refusal Cone Structure and Cross-Lingual Representational Independence

The analyses above use a single mean-difference direction $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ , whereas Wollschläger et al. (2025) show for English that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional concept cones. We extend this to the multilingual setting via (i) activation-domain cone optimisation, fitting the cone basis directly on cached residual activations rather than through gradient-based model interventions, and (ii) Cross-Lingual Representational Independence (CL-RepInd) between refusal basis directions.

##### Cone optimisation.

Let $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ be an orthonormal basis for an $N$ -dimensional refusal cone, seeded with $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ . $\mathbf{B}$ is optimised to maximise the harmful–harmless margin along each basis direction on English activations while penalising margin collapse on non-English activations:

| | $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})=&-\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})}_{\text{EN margin}}+\lambda_{\rm cone}\underbrace{\vphantom{\frac{1}{N}}\bigl({\rm ReLU}(\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})-\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i-1}))\bigr)}_{\text{cone spread}}\\
&-\lambda_{\rm xl}\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\Delta_{\lambda}(b_{i})}_{\text{CL margin}},\end{split}$
| | (3)

where $\Delta_{\lambda}(b)$ is the harmful–harmless margin along $b$ for language $\lambda$ and $\Lambda$ is the set of non-English languages. We use Stiefel-manifold gradient ascent for 400 steps ( $\eta\!=\!0.05$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{cone}}\!=\!5$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{xl}}\!=\!1$ ), fitting $N\!\in\!\{1,\ldots,5\}$ and treating $N\!=\!5$ as canonical. CL-RepInd is the Pearson correlation of the per-language margin vectors of two basis directions.

##### Results (Figures 5–6,
Appendix D).

The first basis direction $b_{0}$ attains large English margins (Qwen:  $9.7$ ; Aya:  $6.1$ ; Llama:  $2.8$ ) and substantial cross-lingual margins ( $5.3$ , $3.8$ , $0.75$ ). Beyond $b_{0}$ , mean margins decay steeply: by dimension three the minimum sampled cone margin is near zero for all models. Cross-lingual margins for $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ are near zero or negative (Aya $b_{1}$ : $-0.4$ ; Qwen $b_{1}$ : $-0.9$ ), so secondary directions degrade non-English separation. CL-RepInd gives $|r|<0.2$ among $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ , with language-cluster-specific structure: on Aya, $b_{1}$ has negative margins for Japanese and Korean; on Qwen, $b_{2}$ singles out Arabic. Cross-lingual refusal is effectively one-dimensional.

Even $b_{0}$ shows near-zero margins for Tier-4 languages on all three models; Tier-4 failures accordingly call for intervention at the harmfulness-detection stage rather than in the refusal subspace.

## 6 Discussion

Multilingual jailbreak vulnerability decomposes into failure modes determined by the manipulation applied. Semantic recovery failure predominates in transliteration of non-Latin-script languages and in very-low-resource Tier-4 languages; subthreshold activation predominates in Tier-3 standard translation and translationese. Code-switching constitutes a third mode, disruption of language-identification routing, independent of representation quality.

##### Refusal geometry is effectively one-dimensional cross-lingually.

The English refusal cone is multi-dimensional per Wollschläger et al. (2025), but only $b_{0}$ transfers cross-lingually; $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ carry near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins on all three models and encode script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. Geometry-aware safety interventions (contrastive activation addition, refusal subspace projection) can be expected to generalise cross-lingually only along $b_{0}$ , and interventions along higher cone dimensions may degrade non-English safety. The per-language margin heatmaps mirror the script-conditioned bimodality of Section 4.2.

##### Tier-4 failure is upstream, not directional.

Near-zero $b_{0}$ margins for Tier-4 languages place the failure in the harm representation rather than the orientation of the refusal axis, requiring upstream interventions at the harmfulness-detection stage. Swahili is a Tier-3 outlier with consistently near-zero $b_{0}$ margins across all models: fluency and safety alignment can decouple during training, and resource tier is an imperfect proxy for safety risk.

##### Cross-model consistency.

The tier gradient, script-conditioned bimodality, geometric decoupling of harm and refusal, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal replicate across Llama, Qwen, and Aya, indicating structural properties of transformer safety alignment under multilingual distribution shift rather than model-specific artifacts. Extended limitations and future work directions are in Appendix F.

## 7 Conclusion

We introduced Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types, evaluated across three instruction-tuned models. Attack-type vulnerability profiles are structurally distinct and irreducible to resource level: transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned, code-switching maintains effectiveness through Tier 4, and translationese consistently amplifies standard translation ASR. The safety regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3 is sharp and replicable across all three models.

Harmful content in low-resource languages occupies a geometrically thinner, less linearly separable subspace whose principal angles with the English harmfulness subspace approach orthogonality at Tier 4, and usable harm representations frequently fail to exceed the decision threshold along the refusal direction (subthreshold activation), consistently across all three architectures.

The English refusal cone is multi-dimensional but cross-linguistically thin: only $b_{0}$ transfers robustly across languages, while secondary directions carry near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins and appear to encode script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. Only $b_{0}$ -aligned additions can be expected to boost refusal cross-lingually; interventions along higher cone dimensions risk degrading non-English safety.

The consistency of these failure modes across Llama, Qwen, and Aya, with their differing multilingual training regimes, has direct implications for the design of safety audits and governance frameworks for global deployment. English-only safety testing, or testing that ignores perturbation type, script family, and per-language alignment coverage, is insufficient to surface the vulnerability profile documented here.

## Impact Statement

This paper aims to improve the safety and equity of multilingual LLM deployment by exposing how models that refuse harmful prompts in English may still comply in lower-resource languages or under perturbations such as transliteration, code-switching, and translationese. By introducing Minionese and analyzing these failures mechanistically, we provide diagnostic tools for multilingual safety evaluation, red-teaming, and future alignment interventions. While this work makes vulnerable language–attack combinations accessible, we mitigate this risk by emphasizing failure mechanisms rather than optimized attack recipes or harmful completions. Overall, we believe that measuring these gaps is necessary for responsible deployment, since English-only safety testing can obscure risks faced by non-English and low-resource language communities.

## Appendix A Extended Related Work

### A.1 Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmarks and the Low-Resource Safety Gap

Deng et al. (2024) first systematically characterized the cross-lingual fragility of safety alignment, finding that low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages in both unintentional and intentional jailbreak scenarios. Their benchmark, MultiJail, restricts the attack surface to standard translation. Zou et al. (2023) provide AdvBench, the English benchmark of harmful behaviors on which subsequent multilingual studies build; their greedy-gradient suffix attack shows that aligned models remain adversarially brittle in their primary training language. Chao et al. (2024) address reproducibility in jailbreak evaluation with a standardized, open-sourced benchmark and unified threat model, again English-only.

Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) demonstrate that fine-tuning an LLM on entirely harmless data in a new, low-resource language suffices to jailbreak it, attributing the effect to late-layer pivots that override safety-critical representations with language-fidelity objectives, an indirect form of the semantic-recovery failure we study under transliteration. Poppi et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning attacks generalize cross-lingually: compromising a model in one language degrades its safety in others, with only approximately 20% of weight parameters implicated, suggesting that safety information is largely language-agnostic at the parameter level.

Wang et al. (2025) construct a 14-language dataset of translated harmful prompts and show that refusal directions extracted from English transfer with near-perfect effectiveness to other languages, with refusal vectors approximately parallel in activation space; insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English languages accounts for the persistence of cross-lingual jailbreaks despite a universal refusal direction.

Minionese varies the type of linguistic manipulation (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese) while holding semantic content constant, rather than treating language identity as the sole independent variable. This supports a per-attack-type mechanistic analysis that neither MultiJail nor PolyRefuse affords, and shows that the attack types exploit distinct representational failure modes rather than a single uniform vulnerability.

### A.2 The Refusal Mechanism in Large Language Models

Arditi et al. (2024) established that refusal in aligned LLMs is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction in activation space: ablating it suppresses refusal on harmful inputs, and adding it induces refusal on benign ones. The result was first shown in English and underlies subsequent jailbreak and defense methods.

Wollschläger et al. (2025) show via gradient-based representation engineering that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones, infinite families of directions each capable of mediating refusal, and that both linear and nonlinear effects must be accounted for to identify genuinely distinct mechanisms. Zhao et al. (2025) extract a harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a refusal direction at the post-instruction token, and show causally that they are separable: models may retain an internal belief that an input is harmful under jailbreaks that successfully suppress refusal outputs.

## Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

### F.1 Limitations

All perturbation types rely on Google Translate; translation quality varies substantially across language pairs, and systematic errors may introduce confounds, particularly for transliteration. Evaluation uses WildGuard as the sole primary judge with NLLB-200 back-translation for non-English responses; back-translation quality degrades for very-low-resource languages, potentially biasing Tier-4 ASR estimates. The geometric analysis is confined to linear probing and mean-difference refusal directions, which may miss nonlinear safety mechanisms, and is carried out on the standard translation condition; the mapping of transliteration and code-switching onto specific failure modes rests on behavioral evidence. Only 8B-scale models are evaluated, and whether the tier gradients, script-conditioned bimodality, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal generalise to larger models is open. Attribution of behavioural patterns to representational mechanisms remains correlational; direct causal verification via activation patching is left to future work.

### F.2 Future Work

Activation and path patching would directly test the language-identification disruption hypothesis for code-switching and localise the layers responsible for subthreshold activation failure. Contrastive activation addition along $b_{0}$ is the only geometry-aware repair likely to generalise cross-lingually; whether boosting harmful-activation projections onto $b_{0}$ remediates Tier-3 failures without collapsing multilingual fluency is a concrete next step. The benchmark can be expanded to additional script families (Ethiopic, further Devanagari languages) and attack types (phonetic perturbation, homoglyph substitution). The script-family structure in secondary cone directions $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ warrants dedicated analysis to isolate which training examples give rise to these language-cluster-specific refusal sub-circuits.

###### Abstract

Safety alignment in large language models remains brittle across languages: prompts reliably refused in English can elicit harmful compliance in non-English and low-resource settings. We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 perturbation types (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese), built on matched harmful–harmless prompt pairs, together with a geometric analysis of refusal failure across language tiers. Each attack type yields a distinct vulnerability profile: transliteration vulnerability tracks script identity, code-switching remains effective through the lowest-resource tier, and all models show a sharp safety regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3. In the residual stream, harmfulness subspaces for lower-resource languages sit at large principal angles to their English counterparts, approaching orthogonality at Tier 4, while probe decodability of harm persists through Tier 3; failures classify as mixed or upstream, never downstream, and only the leading refusal-cone direction carries positive cross-lingual margin. English-only safety evaluations are therefore insufficient; they must account for script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage. The benchmark and analysis code is at https://github.com/Brentkong/Minionese-Comprehensive-Benchmark-and-Mechanistic-Study-of-Multilingual-LLM-Safety.git.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, where they are expected to remain both helpful and safe across languages, scripts, and user populations. In practice, LLMs behave less reliably in non-English and low-resource language contexts owing to disparities in training data, evaluation coverage, and representational fidelity (Pava and others, 2025). Users in lower-resource language communities consequently receive weaker safety guarantees than English users, and current evaluation frameworks largely fail to surface the disparity. Closing this gap requires moving beyond aggregate jailbreak rates toward an account of where and why safety enforcement degrades under multilingual distribution shift.

Multilingual prompting can substantially amplify jailbreak success rates (Deng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), yet the corresponding failure modes are poorly characterized at the level of internal model behavior. In English-centric settings, refusal can be mediated by a low-dimensional direction in activation space: ablating it suppresses refusal on harmful requests, and adding it induces refusal on benign ones (Arditi et al., 2024). Wang et al. (2025) further show that refusal among safety-aligned languages is mediated by a single direction, and that multilingual jailbreaks persist despite this shared mechanism because harmful and harmless prompts are less cleanly separated in non-English representation spaces (Wang et al., 2025).

We do not re-establish the universality of refusal directions. Instead, we ask where the refusal trigger fails under meaning-preserving perturbations an attacker would realistically employ, and what geometry accompanies that failure. Our stress suite extends standard translation with code-switching, transliteration, and translationese across 18 languages and 4 resource tiers.

We separate harmfulness detection from refusal activation in the residual stream, following the instruction-token / post-instruction-token decomposition of Zhao et al. (2025). Principal angles between low-resource and English harmfulness subspaces approach orthogonality at Tier 4. Through Tier 3, harm remains linearly decodable at high AUC in conditions with elevated ASR, which we term subthreshold activation. At Tier 4, probe AUC degrades toward chance, which we term semantic recovery failure. Romanization of non-Latin-script languages produces the highest ASR of any attack in Tiers 1–2. Code-switching ASR is largely insensitive to resource tier, which we attribute to disruption of language-identification routing.

Script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage are therefore necessary variables in AI Safety evaluation and alignment methods. Our contributions are as follows:

1.

We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types, with harmful-harmless prompt pairs enabling per-attack-type mechanistic analysis that prior translation-only benchmarks do not support.

2.

We evaluate three instruction-tuned models and find distinct, replicable vulnerability profiles per attack type: script-conditioned transliteration vulnerability, code-switching effectiveness through Tier 4, and a sharp Tier 2–3 safety regime transition consistent across all models.

3.

We develop a geometric framework separating harmfulness detection from refusal activation in the residual stream, comprising per-language probe AUC, silhouette scores, principal angles between harmfulness subspaces, harm/refusal signal correlations, layer-wise failure classification, and a multilingual refusal-cone decomposition with a cross-lingual independence metric. This framework yields evidence for two failure modes, subthreshold activation and semantic recovery failure.

## 2 Related Work

##### Multilingual jailbreak benchmarks.

Deng et al. (2024) established the language-safety gap empirically, showing that low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages. Subsequent benchmarks tightened evaluation standards (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024) but remain confined to English. Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) show that fine-tuning on harmless low-resource data suffices to jailbreak a model, and Poppi et al. (2025) show that safety degradation transfers cross-lingually through only roughly 20% of model parameters. Closest to our work, Wang et al. (2025) construct a 14-language translated-prompt dataset, show that refusal directions transfer across languages, and attribute persistent jailbreaks to insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English spaces. Minionese instead treats linguistic manipulation type (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) as an independent variable, which supports per-attack-type mechanistic analysis.

##### The refusal mechanism.

Arditi et al. (2024) showed that refusal is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction in activation space, the basis of subsequent jailbreak and defense methods. Wollschläger et al. (2025) show that refusal is instead governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones. Zhao et al. (2025) identify a harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a separate refusal direction at the post-instruction token, with causal evidence that the two dissociate under jailbreaks. We carry the harmfulness detection / refusal activation distinction into the multilingual domain. Appendix A extends this discussion.

## 3 Minionese: A Granular Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmark

Existing multilingual benchmarks treat language identity as the primary variable and restrict their attack surface to standard translation. Minionese holds semantic content constant and varies the type of linguistic manipulation applied to it.

##### Base corpus.

Minionese is built on the 385 harmful prompts from AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023). For each harmful prompt, ChatGPT’s GPT-5.4 produces a matched harmless counterpart by replacing harmful phrases with semantically parallel benign substitutes, yielding 385 harmful-harmless prompt pairs. Human reviewers verified that each harmless prompt preserves the sentence structure and length of its harmful pair.

##### Languages and resource tiers.

The benchmark spans 18 languages grouped into four resource tiers according to training-data availability in contemporary LLMs:

•

Tier 1 (high-resource): English, Spanish, Chinese, German,
French

•

Tier 2 (mid-high resource): Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese

•

Tier 3 (mid-low resource): Turkish, Indonesian, Hindi, Swahili

•

Tier 4 (low-resource): Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní,
Javanese

All translations use the Google Translate API. Each of the four attack types is applied to every harmful-harmless pair in all 18 languages, for $385\times 2\times 4\times 18=55,440$ total prompts. Examples of each attack type are given in Section E of the appendix.

### 3.1 Attack Types

##### Standard translation.

Each harmful-harmless prompt pair is translated in full into the target language. This condition replicates the setting of prior multilingual jailbreak studies.

##### Code-switching.

Each pair is tokenized into words and punctuation marks, and the contiguous span on which the harmful and harmless prompts differ is identified. Only the alphabetic tokens within that span are translated into the target language; all shared context outside the span remains in English.

##### Transliteration.

Each prompt is first translated into the target language and then script-converted, preserving pronunciation while discarding native orthography. Prompts in non-Romance languages are romanized into Latin characters, and prompts in Romance languages are rendered in Latin-Cyrillic.

##### Translationese.

The English prompt is translated into the target language, back-translated into English, and translated into the target language again, three translation steps in total. The final prompt is in the target language and carries the surface statistics of machine-translated text.

## 4 Evaluation

We evaluate three models on all 18 languages and 4 perturbation types in Minionese, measuring attack success rate (ASR), response coherence, and safety regime distribution. The pipeline has three stages: response generation, coherence filtering, and safety scoring via back-translated WildGuard judgments.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### 4.1.1 Models and Inference

We evaluate Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Aya-Expanse-8B, all with greedy decoding (temperature $=0$ ) and at most 512 new tokens.

#### 4.1.2 Coherence Filtering

For each (model, language, perturbation) triple, we generate responses to all 385 harmful and 385 harmless prompts. Each response is scored for coherence using language identification (langdetect) and Unicode validity. A response is incoherent if (i) its detected language matches neither the target language nor English; (ii) language identification confidence is below 0.3; (iii) Unicode validity is below 0.8; or (iv) the response is under 20 characters long. Incoherent responses are excluded from ASR computation. Coherence rates are at or near 1.0 across all conditions (see Section 4.2).

#### 4.1.3 Attack Success Rate Measurement

WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) is the primary safety judge. Non-English responses are back-translated to English before scoring, to mitigate WildGuard’s reduced reliability on non-English text. A response counts as an attack success if WildGuard does not classify it as a refusal. ASR is the fraction of harmful prompts eliciting compliant responses within each (language, perturbation, model) cell:

| | $\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{model}(x)\ \text{is compliant}\right],$
| | (1)

where $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}$ is the set of harmful prompts and $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function. We report ASR per language, per perturbation type, and aggregated by resource tier, together with $\Delta$ ASR relative to the English baseline.

### 4.2 Results

Figure 1: ASR by language and perturbation type, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Heatmaps for
Aya and Qwen are in Appendix B.

Figure 1 shows per-language, per-attack-type ASR for Llama; Qwen and Aya show similar qualitative patterns (Appendix B).

#### 4.2.1 Attack Type and Tier Profiles

##### Standard translation and translationese follow a tier gradient.

For both attack types, ASR rises substantially as resource level falls on all three models. Under standard translation, Llama mean ASR rises from approximately 8% in Tier 1 to over 70% in Tiers 3–4 (Yoruba 100%, Zulu 97%, Scottish Gaelic 98%). Qwen follows the same pattern (Swahili 96%, Scottish Gaelic 90%, Yoruba 75%). Aya shows a more moderate gradient, except for Swahili at 95%. Translationese exceeds standard translation ASR at mid-resource languages, most strongly for Korean (14% vs. 51% on Aya) and Hindi (15% vs. 48% on Llama). This is consistent with round-trip translation shifting phrasing toward naturalistic surface forms that weaken harmfulness detection upstream.

##### Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned.

For non-Latin-script languages in Tiers 1–2, transliteration yields the highest ASR of any attack type: Korean reaches 98% on Aya and 99% on Llama, Chinese 97% on Llama, Arabic 84% on Aya, and Hindi 99% on Llama. For Latin-script and very-low-resource Tier-4 languages, transliteration ASR drops to near zero (French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on both Aya and Qwen). On Qwen, $\Delta$ ASR is negative for Yoruba ( $-38\%$ ), Russian ( $-48\%$ ), and Scottish Gaelic ( $-44\%$ ). The same bimodality appears on all three models.

##### Code-switching produces the most tier-stable attack profile.

Code-switching sustains moderate-to-high ASR across all resource tiers and models. Tier-4 code-switching ASR stays elevated where other attack types are near zero: Yoruba (62% on Aya, 82% on Llama), Zulu (62% on Aya, 85% on Llama), and Guaraní (42% on Aya, 46% on Llama). A tier gradient is present but substantially shallower than under standard translation, which we attribute to disruption of language-identification routing.

##### The safety regime transitions sharply between Tiers 2 and 3.

All three models predominantly refuse in Tiers 1–2: Llama refuses 80% in Tier 1 and 75% in Tier 2, Qwen 80% and 88%, and Aya 75% in both. At Tier 3, refusal drops to 31% for Llama, 50% for Qwen, and 31% for Aya, and Aya reaches 95% comply by Tier 4. A mixed regime is nearly absent across all models and tiers, indicating a threshold effect in refusal activation.

#### 4.2.2 Cross-Model Consistency

Qualitative vulnerability profiles agree across models while absolute magnitudes diverge substantially. The rank ordering of attack types by mean ASR is stable. Transliteration dominates for Tier-1 and Tier-2 non-Latin-script languages, and code-switching dominates at Tier 4. Standard translation and translationese are the most closely matched pair and generally the lowest in ASR.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is the most broadly vulnerable model, with Tier-4 standard translation mean ASR approaching 80%, against approximately 55% for Qwen and 35% for Aya. The script-conditioned bimodality in transliteration reproduces across all three architectures (Appendix B), which locates it in the romanization operation rather than in any single model.

## 5 Geometric Analysis of Refusal

We decompose multilingual jailbreak vulnerability into upstream (detection) and downstream (refusal activation) stages and operationalize the split through linear probing, subspace construction, and cross-lingual transfer analysis.

### 5.1 Preliminaries

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a transformer with $L$ layers and hidden dimension $d$ . We extract residual stream activations $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ at the last post-instruction token position $t^{*}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$ . For language $\lambda$ and layer $\ell$ , the paired benchmark gives harmful and harmless activation sets $\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ and $\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ .

##### Harmfulness subspace.

For each $(\lambda,\ell)$ , we train a logistic regression probe and stack its weights across harm categories into $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{C}|}$ , where $\mathcal{C}$ comprises the “all“ and “unknown” categories derived from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024). $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ is the column space of the top- $k$ right singular vectors of $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , with $k$ chosen to explain $\geq 95\%$ of spectral mass.

##### Refusal direction.

$\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is extracted from English activations by contrasting refused ( $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}$ ) and complied ( $\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}$ ) sets:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}\|_{2}}$
| | (2)

##### Failure classification.

Following Zhao et al. (2025), we separate harm and refusal components and label each $(\lambda,\ell)$ pair as upstream, downstream, or mixed. Refusal is modeled as $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)\top}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})>\tau^{(\ell)}$ with $\tau^{(\ell)}=0.95$ .

### 5.2 Results

##### Harmful-harmless separation degrades with resource tier.

Figure 2 reports silhouette scores (Rousseeuw, 1987) in the harmfulness-subspace-projected residual stream. Tier-1 and Tier-2 languages keep high, stable separation across the full layer range on all three models. Separation declines from Tier 3 onward, consistently across architectures. Guaraní (gn) is the extreme case, with near-zero and negative silhouette scores across all layers on all models. Swahili (sw) is a within-tier outlier, with separation substantially below other Tier-3 languages on all three models, matching its anomalously high ASR (Section 4.2).

The tier ordering is fixed by mid-network depth and stays stable thereafter, and lower-resource languages do not regain separation in later layers. The absolute Tier-1-to-Tier-4 gap is consistent across architectures and largest for Aya.

Figure 3: Linear probe AUC for harmfulness detection across all layers using standard_translation attack type
(category all; chance $=0.5$ ).

##### Probe AUC confirms subthreshold activation as the dominant failure mode.

Figure 3 shows 5-fold cross-validated probe AUC across the full layer range. All three models reach AUC ${\geq}0.85$ from early layers onward for Tiers 1–3. Degradation is concentrated in Tier 4, where Yoruba and Zulu approach chance in late layers on all models.

For Tier-3 languages, probe AUC stays high even in language-perturbation conditions with elevated ASR. For Tier-4 languages, AUC falls toward chance, consistent with semantic recovery failure.

Figure 4: Principal angle between non-English and English safety subspaces as a
function of normalized layer depth, per tier and model for standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmfulness subspaces are not cross-lingually universal.

Figure 4 plots the first principal angle $\theta^{(\ell)}_{\lambda,1}$ between non-English and English harmfulness subspaces against normalized layer depth. No tier comes near $0^{\circ}$ . Tier-1 languages sit at $40$ – $65^{\circ}$ depending on the model, and Tier-4 languages approach near-orthogonality ( ${\sim}85$ – $90^{\circ}$ ) on all three architectures. The angles are broadly stable across depth, with no late-layer cross-lingual realignment. Qwen has the smallest mean angles ( ${\approx}60$ – $65^{\circ}$ ), matching its comparatively higher Tier-4 silhouette scores in Figure 2.

The principal angles increase monotonically from Tier 1 to Tier 4, paralleling the ASR tier gradient.

##### Harm and refusal signals are geometrically decoupled.

Figure 9 (Appendix C) gives four views of the harmfulness-refusal decomposition for all three models. Harm and refusal component norms are weakly correlated and widely scattered on every model. Swahili, Scottish Gaelic, Yoruba, and Zulu each show instances, across the models, of a disproportionately large harm norm relative to the refusal component. For Aya and Llama, the per-language contrastive harm signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{harm}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{inst}}$ correlates strongly negatively with the refusal signal $\sigma_{\mathrm{refusal}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{post}}$ , with $r=-0.79$ for Aya and $r=-0.68$ for Llama. Qwen instead shows a positive correlation, $r=+0.53$ . The universality of Tier-4 language clusters in the low-harm, variable-refusal region across further models remains open.

Layer-wise failure classification is predominantly mixed on all three models. A small number of upstream classifications appear in Tier-4 languages. No model shows any downstream failure.

##### Synthesis.

The three models agree. Tier-1 inputs show clean harmful-harmless separation and adequate projection onto $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ . For Tier-3–4 inputs, one or both of these fail. The dominant label is mixed: a usable harmfulness representation is present at the instruction token, but it lies in a misaligned, low-rank subspace whose intersection with $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ does not clear the threshold. In the lowest-resource Tier-4 languages, the harm representation additionally degrades toward chance. $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}$ itself is not destroyed.

### 5.3 Refusal Cone Structure and Cross-Lingual Representational Independence

Sections 5.1–5.2 use a single mean-difference direction $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ . Wollschläger et al. (2025) show for English-centric settings that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional concept cones. We carry this framework into the multilingual domain in two ways. First, we fit the cone basis directly on cached residual activations rather than through gradient-based model interventions. Second, we introduce Cross-Lingual Representational Independence (CL-RepInd).

##### Cone optimisation.

Let $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ be an orthonormal basis for an $N$ -dimensional refusal cone, seeded with $\hat{r}^{(\ell)}$ , optimised as:

| | $\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{B})=&-\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})}_{\text{EN margin}}+\lambda_{\rm cone}\underbrace{\vphantom{\frac{1}{N}}\bigl({\rm ReLU}(\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i})-\Delta_{\rm en}(b_{i-1}))\bigr)}_{\text{cone spread}}\\
&-\lambda_{\rm xl}\underbrace{\frac{1}{|\Lambda|}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\Delta_{\lambda}(b_{i})}_{\text{CL margin}},\end{split}$
| | (3)

where $\Delta_{\lambda}(b)$ is the harmful–harmless margin along $b$ for language $\lambda$ and $\Lambda$ is the set of non-English languages. We run Stiefel-manifold gradient ascent for 400 steps ( $\eta\!=\!0.05$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{cone}}\!=\!5$ , $\lambda_{\mathrm{xl}}\!=\!1$ ), fit $N\!\in\!\{1,\ldots,5\}$ , and take $N\!=\!5$ as canonical. CL-RepInd is the Pearson correlation of the per-language margin vectors of two basis directions.

##### Results (Figures 5–6,
Appendix D).

The first basis direction $b_{0}$ attains large English margins (Qwen:  $9.7$ ; Aya:  $6.1$ ; Llama:  $2.8$ ) and substantial cross-lingual margins ( $5.3$ , $3.8$ , $0.75$ ). Beyond $b_{0}$ , mean margins decay steeply, and by dimension three the minimum sampled cone margin is near zero for all models. Cross-lingual margins for $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ are near zero or negative (Aya $b_{1}$ : $-0.4$ ; Qwen $b_{1}$ : $-0.9$ ). CL-RepInd gives $|r|<0.2$ among $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ , each of which picks out language-cluster-specific structure: on Aya, $b_{1}$ has negative margins for Japanese and Korean, and on Qwen, $b_{2}$ singles out Arabic. Cross-lingual refusal is effectively one-dimensional.

Even $b_{0}$ shows near-zero margins for Tier-4 languages on all three models, so the Tier-4 failure is upstream. Patching Tier-4 failures requires intervening at the harmfulness-detection stage, not in the refusal subspace.

## 6 Discussion

Multilingual jailbreak vulnerability decomposes by manipulation type. Semantic recovery failure predominates in transliteration of non-Latin-script languages and in Tier-4 languages. Subthreshold activation predominates in Tier-3 standard translation and translationese. Code-switching corresponds to disruption of language-identification routing, independent of representation quality.

##### Refusal geometry is effectively one-dimensional cross-lingually.

The English refusal cone is multi-dimensional per Wollschläger et al. (2025), but only $b_{0}$ transfers cross-lingually (Section 5.3). Secondary directions $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ carry near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins on all three models and encode script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. Geometry-aware safety interventions, such as contrastive activation addition and refusal subspace projection, can be expected to generalise cross-lingually only along $b_{0}$ , and interventions along higher cone dimensions may degrade non-English safety. The per-language margin heatmaps mirror the script-conditioned bimodality of Section 4.2, which points to a shared geometric origin for surface vulnerability and cone structure.

##### Tier-4 failure is upstream, not directional.

Even $b_{0}$ shows near-zero margins for Tier-4 languages, and patching them requires upstream intervention at the harmfulness-detection stage. Swahili, a Tier-3 language, has consistently near-zero $b_{0}$ margins on all models, which indicates that fluency and safety alignment can decouple during training and that resource tier is an imperfect proxy for safety risk.

##### Cross-model consistency.

The tier gradient, script-conditioned bimodality, geometric decoupling of harm and refusal, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal all replicate across Llama, Qwen, and Aya. These failure modes reflect structural properties of transformer safety alignment under multilingual distribution shift rather than model-specific artifacts. Appendix F gives extended limitations and future work.

## 7 Conclusion

We introduced Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types, and evaluated it on three instruction-tuned models. Attack-type vulnerability profiles are structurally distinct and not reducible to resource level. Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned, code-switching remains effective through Tier 4, and translationese consistently amplifies standard translation ASR. The Tier 2–3 safety regime transition is sharp and replicates across all three models.

The geometric analysis gives a two-stage failure account that holds on all three architectures. Harmful content in low-resource languages occupies a geometrically thinner, less linearly separable subspace, whose principal angles with the English harmfulness subspace approach orthogonality at Tier 4. Usable harm representations frequently fail to exceed the refusal decision threshold, which is subthreshold activation.

The English refusal cone is multi-dimensional but cross-linguistically thin. Only $b_{0}$ transfers robustly across languages, while secondary directions carry near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins and appear to encode script-family-specific refusal sub-circuits. As a result, only $b_{0}$ -aligned additions can be expected to boost refusal cross-lingually, and interventions along higher cone dimensions risk degrading non-English safety.

These failure modes are consistent across Llama, Qwen, and Aya despite their differing multilingual training regimes, which bears directly on how safety audits and governance frameworks should be designed for global deployment. Safety testing that is English-only, or that ignores perturbation type, script family, and per-language alignment coverage, is insufficient to surface the vulnerability profile documented here.

## Impact Statement

This paper aims to improve the safety and equity of multilingual LLM deployment by exposing how models that refuse harmful prompts in English may still comply in lower-resource languages or under perturbations such as transliteration, code-switching, and translationese. By introducing Minionese and analyzing these failures mechanistically, we provide diagnostic tools for multilingual safety evaluation, red-teaming, and future alignment interventions. While this work makes vulnerable language–attack combinations accessible, we mitigate this risk by emphasizing failure mechanisms rather than optimized attack recipes or harmful completions. Overall, we believe that measuring these gaps is necessary for responsible deployment, since English-only safety testing can obscure risks faced by non-English and low-resource language communities.

## Appendix A Extended Related Work

### A.1 Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmarks and the Low-Resource Safety Gap

Deng et al. (2024) first systematically characterized the fragility of LLM safety alignment across languages. They showed that low-resource languages produce unsafe outputs at roughly three times the rate of high-resource languages in both unintentional and intentional jailbreak scenarios. Their benchmark, MultiJail, restricts its attack surface to standard translation. On the English side, Zou et al. (2023) provide AdvBench, the benchmark of harmful behaviors on which subsequent multilingual studies build, and their greedy-gradient suffix attack shows that aligned models remain adversarially brittle in their primary training language. Chao et al. (2024) address reproducibility in jailbreak evaluation with a standardized, open-sourced benchmark and unified threat model, also English-only. These resources set rigorous evaluation standards but leave the multilingual dimension underspecified.

Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) show that fine-tuning an LLM on entirely harmless data in a new, low-resource language suffices to jailbreak the model. They attribute the effect to late-layer pivots in which language-fidelity objectives override safety-critical representations, an indirect form of the semantic-recovery failure we study in the transliteration condition. Poppi et al. (2025) show that fine-tuning attacks generalize cross-lingually. Compromising a model in one language degrades its safety in others, with only approximately 20% of weight parameters implicated, which suggests that safety information is largely language-agnostic at the parameter level.

Wang et al. (2025) construct a 14-language dataset of translated harmful prompts. They show that refusal directions extracted from English transfer with near-perfect effectiveness to other languages, with refusal vectors approximately parallel in activation space, and that insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English languages accounts for cross-lingual jailbreaks persisting despite a universal refusal direction.

Minionese departs from this line by varying the type of linguistic manipulation (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, and translationese) at fixed semantic content, rather than treating language identity as the sole independent variable. This supports a per-attack-type mechanistic analysis that neither MultiJail nor PolyRefuse affords and that separates attack types by representational failure mode.

### A.2 The Refusal Mechanism in Large Language Models

Arditi et al. (2024) showed that refusal in aligned LLMs is mediated by a single low-dimensional direction in activation space: ablating it suppresses refusal on harmful inputs, and adding it induces refusal on benign ones. This English result underlies subsequent jailbreak and defense methods.

Wollschläger et al. (2025) use gradient-based representation engineering to show that refusal is governed by multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones, infinite families of directions each capable of mediating refusal, and that identifying genuinely distinct mechanisms requires accounting for both linear and nonlinear effects. Zhao et al. (2025) extract a harmfulness direction at the instruction token and a refusal direction at the post-instruction token and show causally that the two are separable. Models may retain an internal belief that an input is harmful under jailbreaks that successfully suppress refusal outputs.

## Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

### F.1 Limitations

All perturbation types rely on Google Translate. Translation quality varies substantially across language pairs, and systematic errors may introduce confounds, particularly for transliteration. Evaluation uses WildGuard as the sole primary judge, with NLLB-200 back-translation for non-English responses. Back-translation quality degrades for very-low-resource languages, which may bias Tier-4 ASR estimates. The geometric analysis is confined to linear probing and mean-difference refusal directions and may miss nonlinear safety mechanisms. Only 8B-scale models are evaluated, and it remains open whether the tier gradients, script-conditioned bimodality, and effective one-dimensionality of cross-lingual refusal generalise to larger models. Causal attribution of behavioural patterns to representational mechanisms remains correlational, and direct verification via activation patching is left to future work.

### F.2 Future Work

The most immediate extension is causal attribution via activation and path patching, which would test the language-identification disruption hypothesis for code-switching and localise the layers responsible for subthreshold activation failure. A second direction is targeted intervention. Contrastive activation addition along $b_{0}$ is the only geometry-aware repair likely to generalise cross-lingually, and a concrete next step is to evaluate systematically whether boosting harmful-activation projections onto $b_{0}$ remediates Tier-3 failures without collapsing multilingual fluency. A third direction is expanding the benchmark to additional script families (Ethiopic, further Devanagari languages) and attack types (phonetic perturbation, homoglyph substitution). Finally, the script-family structure in secondary cone directions $b_{1}$ – $b_{4}$ warrants dedicated analysis to identify which training examples give rise to these language-cluster-specific refusal sub-circuits.

# Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety

Chigozirim Ifebi

Affiliation: California Institute of Technology

Correspondence to: cifebi@caltech.edu

###### Abstract

We introduce Minionese, a multilingual jailbreak benchmark spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 perturbation types (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese), with a geometric analysis of refusal failure across tiers. Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned, code-switching remains effective through the lowest-resource tier, and a sharp safety-regime transition between Tiers 2 and 3 holds across all models. Low-resource harmful content occupies a subspace geometrically misaligned with, and projecting insufficiently onto, the refusal directions. English-only safety evaluation is insufficient; script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage must be accounted for. Code: https://github.com/Brentkong/Minionese-Comprehensive-Benchmark-and-Mechanistic-Study-of-Multilingual-LLM-Safety.git.

###### Keywords: 

jailbreaking, multilingual jailbreaking, mechanistic interpretability

††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

that can be offensive in nature.

## 1 Introduction

LLMs behave less reliably in non-English and low-resource contexts owing to disparities in training data, evaluation coverage, and representational fidelity (Pava and others, 2025), and lower-resource language communities receive weaker safety guarantees that current evaluation largely fails to surface. Multilingual prompting amplifies jailbreak success (Deng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). In English, ablating a low-dimensional activation direction suppresses refusal on harmful requests and adding it induces refusal on benign ones (Arditi et al., 2024). Refusal among safety-aligned languages is mediated by a single direction, and multilingual jailbreaks persist under this shared mechanism given weaker harmful–harmless separation in non-English representation spaces (Wang et al., 2025).

We study where the refusal trigger fails under meaning-preserving perturbations an attacker would employ (code-switching, transliteration, translationese, in addition to standard translation) across 18 languages and 4 resource tiers, separating harmfulness detection from refusal activation in the residual stream. Principal angles between low-resource and English harmfulness subspaces approach orthogonality at Tier 4; harm representations present at the instruction token frequently fall below the refusal decision threshold (subthreshold activation); romanization of non-Latin-script languages yields semantic recovery failure; code-switching is attributed to language-identification routing disruption largely independent of representation quality, matching its effectiveness across all tiers. Script family, perturbation type, and per-language alignment coverage are therefore necessary variables in safety evaluation and alignment. Contributions:

1.

Minionese, spanning 18 languages, 4 resource tiers, and 4 linguistically-motivated perturbation types, with harmful-harmless prompt pairs supporting per-attack-type mechanistic analysis unavailable in translation-only benchmarks.

2.

An evaluation of three instruction-tuned models showing distinct, replicable per-attack-type profiles: script-conditioned transliteration vulnerability, code-switching effectiveness through Tier 4, and a sharp Tier 2–3 safety regime transition across all models.

3.

A geometric framework separating harmfulness detection from refusal activation in the residual stream, with mechanistic evidence for subthreshold activation and semantic recovery failure.

## 2 Related Work

##### Multilingual jailbreak benchmarks.

Deng et al. (2024) report unsafe-output rates roughly three times higher for low-resource than high-resource languages. Later benchmarks (Zou et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2024) tighten evaluation standards but are English-only. Upadhayay and Behzadan (2025) jailbreak models by fine-tuning on harmless low-resource data; Poppi et al. (2025) find safety degradation transfers cross-lingually through roughly 20% of parameters. Wang et al. (2025) build a 14-language translated-prompt dataset, show refusal directions transfer across languages, and attribute persistent jailbreaks to insufficient harmfulness-harmlessness separation in non-English spaces. Minionese treats manipulation type (standard translation, code-switching, transliteration, translationese) as an independent variable. See Appendix A.

##### The refusal mechanism.

Arditi et al. (2024) locate refusal in a single low-dimensional direction; Wollschläger et al. (2025) find multi-dimensional polyhedral concept cones; Zhao et al. (2025) separate a harmfulness direction at the instruction token from a refusal direction at the post-instruction token, with causal evidence of dissociation under jailbreaks. We carry the harmfulness detection / refusal activation distinction into the multilingual setting (Appendix A).

## 3 Minionese: A Granular Multilingual Jailbreak Benchmark

Minionese holds semantic content constant and varies the type of linguistic manipulation, in contrast to benchmarks that vary language identity under standard translation only.

##### Base corpus.

Each of the 385 harmful AdvBench prompts (Zou et al., 2023) is paired with a harmless counterpart obtained by substituting semantically parallel benign phrases via ChatGPT’s GPT-5.4, giving 385 harmful-harmless pairs; human reviewers verified preservation of sentence structure and length.

##### Languages and resource tiers.

18 languages, tiered by training-data availability in contemporary LLMs:

•

Tier 1 (high-resource): English, Spanish, Chinese, German,
French

•

Tier 2 (mid-high resource): Arabic, Russian, Korean, Japanese

•

Tier 3 (mid-low resource): Turkish, Indonesian, Hindi, Swahili

•

Tier 4 (low-resource): Yoruba, Zulu, Scottish Gaelic, Guaraní,
Javanese

Translations use the Google Translate API. All four attack types are applied to every pair in all 18 languages: $385\times 2\times 4\times 18=55,440$ prompts. Examples in Section E of the appendix.

### 3.1 Attack Types

##### Standard translation.

Full-prompt translation of each pair into the target language; the baseline condition, replicating prior multilingual jailbreak studies.

##### Code-switching.

Each pair is tokenized into words and punctuation; the contiguous differing span is identified and only its alphabetic tokens are translated, with shared context left in English.

##### Transliteration.

Translation followed by phonetic script conversion that discards native orthography: Romanization for non-Romance languages, Latin-Cyrillic rendering for Romance languages. Targets refusal operating on script or token identity rather than semantic content.

##### Translationese.

EN $\to$ target $\to$ EN $\to$ target, three translation steps in total; the output is in the target language with machine-translation surface statistics.

## 4 Evaluation

Three models, all 18 languages, all 4 perturbation types; metrics are ASR, response coherence, and safety regime distribution. Pipeline: generation, coherence filtering, back-translated WildGuard scoring.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### 4.1.1 Models and Inference

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Aya-Expanse-8B; greedy decoding (temperature $=0$ ), at most 512 new tokens.

#### 4.1.2 Coherence Filtering

For each (model, language, perturbation) triple, responses are generated for all 385 harmful and 385 harmless prompts. Responses are excluded from ASR as incoherent if (i) the langdetect language matches neither target nor English; (ii) identification confidence is below 0.3; (iii) Unicode validity is below 0.8; or (iv) length is under 20 characters. Coherence is at or near 1.0 in all conditions (Section 4.2).

#### 4.1.3 Attack Success Rate Measurement

Judge: WildGuard (Han et al., 2024), with non-English responses back-translated to English before scoring; non-refusals count as successes. Per (language, perturbation, model) cell:

| | $\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\mathrm{model}(x)\ \text{is compliant}\right],$
| | (1)

with $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{harm}}$ the harmful prompts and $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator. ASR is reported per language, per perturbation, and by tier, together with $\Delta$ ASR against the English baseline.

### 4.2 Results

Figure 1: ASR by language and perturbation type, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Heatmaps for
Aya and Qwen are in Appendix B.

Figure 1 (Llama); Qwen and Aya are qualitatively similar (Appendix B).

#### 4.2.1 Attack Type and Tier Profiles

##### Standard translation and translationese follow a tier gradient.

ASR rises as resource level falls for both, on all three models. Standard translation, Llama: ≈8% mean in Tier 1, over 70% in Tiers 3–4 (Yoruba 100%, Zulu 97%, Scottish Gaelic 98%). Qwen: Swahili 96%, Scottish Gaelic 90%, Yoruba 75%. Aya: a more moderate gradient, except Swahili at 95%. Translationese exceeds standard translation at mid-resource languages, most for Korean (14% vs. 51% on Aya) and Hindi (15% vs. 48% on Llama), consistent with round-trip phrasing weakening harmfulness detection upstream of refusal.

##### Transliteration vulnerability is script-conditioned.

Highest ASR of any attack for non-Latin-script Tier 1–2 languages: Korean 98% (Aya) and 99% (Llama); Chinese 97% (Llama); Arabic 84% (Aya); Hindi 99% (Llama). Near zero for Latin-script and very-low-resource Tier-4 languages (French 0%, Scottish Gaelic 0%, Yoruba 0% on both Aya and Qwen). Qwen $\Delta$ ASR: Yoruba ( $-38\%$ ), Russian ( $-48\%$ ), Scottish Gaelic ( $-44\%$ ). The bimodality replicates across all three models and tracks script identity rather than resource level.

##### Code-switching produces the most tier-stable attack profile.

Moderate-to-high ASR in all tiers and models. Tier 4, where other attacks are near zero: Yoruba (62% Aya, 82% Llama), Zulu (62% Aya, 85% Llama), Guaraní (42% Aya, 46% Llama). The tier gradient is far shallower than under standard translation, consistent with disruption of language-identification routing rather than degraded semantic representation.

##### The safety regime transitions sharply between Tiers 2 and 3.

Refuse rates, Tiers 1/2: Llama 80%/75%; Qwen 80%/88%; Aya 75%/75%. Tier 3: Llama 31%, Qwen 50%, Aya 31%; Aya reaches 95% comply by Tier 4. A mixed regime is nearly absent across models and tiers, consistent with a threshold effect in refusal activation rather than continuous degradation.

#### 4.2.2 Cross-Model Consistency

Rank ordering of attack types by mean ASR is stable across models: transliteration dominates for Tier-1/2 non-Latin-script languages, code-switching at Tier 4, with standard translation and translationese the closest-matched, generally lowest-ASR pair; we take these profiles to reflect structural properties of transformer safety circuits. Magnitudes diverge: Tier-4 standard translation mean ASR approaches 80% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct versus ≈55% for Qwen and 35% for Aya. Transliteration bimodality reproduces on all three architectures (Appendix B), as a property of romanization itself.

## 5 Geometric Analysis of Refusal

Multilingual vulnerability is analyzed as a two-stage failure (upstream detection vs. downstream refusal activation) via linear probing, subspace construction, and cross-lingual transfer.

### 5.1 Preliminaries

$\mathcal{M}$ : transformer with $L$ layers, hidden size $d$ ; $\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ : residual stream at the last post-instruction token $t^{*}$ . $\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , $\mathcal{S}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ : harmful and harmless activation sets for language $\lambda$ , layer $\ell$ .

##### Harmfulness subspace.

Per $(\lambda,\ell)$ , logistic probe weights stacked over categories give $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times|\mathcal{C}|}$ , $\mathcal{C}$ comprising “all “ and “unknown” categories from HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024); $\mathcal{V}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ is the column space of the top- $k$ right singular vectors of $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}_{\lambda}$ , $k$ explaining $\geq 95\%$ of spectral mass.

##### Refusal direction.

From English refused ( $\mathcal{R}^{(\ell)}$ ) and complied ( $\mathcal{C}^{(\ell)}$ ) sets:

| | $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}}{\|\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{R}}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{C}}\|_{2}}$
| | (2)

##### Failure classification.

Following Zhao et al. (2025), each $(\lambda,\ell)$ is labeled upstream (harmfulness subspace too weak to feed refusal), downstream (harm represented, refusal suppressed), or mixed (both attenuated). Refusal fires when $\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{(\ell)\top}\mathbf{h}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{x})>\tau^{(\ell)}$ ; harmful activations with nontrivial harm signal but below $\tau^{(\ell)}=0.95$ constitute subthreshold activation.

### 5.2 Results

Figure 2: Harmful-harmless separation in activation space (silhouette score)
across languages and layers, all three models using standard_translation attack type.

##### Harmful-harmless separation degrades with resource tier.

Silhouette scores (Rousseeuw, 1987) in the harmfulness-subspace-projected residual stream (Figure 2): Tiers 1–2 high and stable across all layers on all models; decline from Tier 3 onward on all architectures. Guaraní (gn) is near zero or negative at all layers on all models, the sharpest degeneration in the benchmark. Swahili (sw) is substantially below other Tier-3 languages on all three models, matching its high ASR (Section 4.2).

Tier ordering is fixed by mid-network depth and persists; no late-layer recovery for lower-resource languages, placing representational quality at encoding rather than depth-specific processing. The Tier-1-to-Tier-4 gap is consistent across architectures, largest on Aya.
